ONE HUNDREDTH ANNIVERSARY OF ITALIAN SETTLEMENT IN CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I crave the indulgence of the house to recognize and do honour to the one hundredth anniversary of Italian settlement in Canada. Tomorrow evening, October 24, in many communities across Canada celebrations will be held to mark the many contributions the Italian people have made to Canada. Indeed, they are the second largest group of people who have emigrated to Canada. Canadians of Italian origin have played a very important part in the development of our country, and as one who has the honour to represent many Italian Canadians I am pleased to recognize this century of their contribution to the economic and social life of Canada.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON SECURITY ARRANGEMENTS FOR ROYAL VISIT

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: STATEMENT ON SECURITY ARRANGEMENTS FOR ROYAL VISIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make the following statement as a result of questions put to me on October 15, 16 and 21 by the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) and the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas).
The prime responsibility of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police was for the safety of Her Majesty the Queen and His Royal Highness the Duke of Edinburgh. A secondary responsibility would have been to furnish assistance to municipal and provincial police in the event that in the maintenance of law and order those forces required assistance from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
So far as the visit to the city of Quebec is concerned, it should be pointed out that for a considerable period prior to the royal visit threats of demonstrations, civil disturbances and violence had been made publicly from anonymous sources.
Several demonstrations occurred, the first one of any consequence being in front of the provincial legislature while Her Majesty was inside the building. These and other demonstrations in the city of Quebec were dealt with by the Quebec city police. The solicitor general of the province of Quebec has issued a statement on these matters.
During the day a number of persons were arrested by the various forces, of whom eight were arrested by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in rendering assistance to the local authorities.
Le Soleil of Quebec city subsequently published a part of the orders issued to members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who were on duty in Quebec city during the royal visit. Individual copies of these orders were issued to all members of the force on duty, and the copy which came into the possession of Le Soleil was not secured from any official source. It has not been possible to ascertain how this particular copy, out of the many that had to be issued, reached the newspaper; but while the document was confidential and for the information of members of the force, there is nothing in it of a secret nature or of a nature affecting security. In fact it exemplifies the care which was taken to see that members of the force were properly instructed. In the circumstances I do not believe that any investigation beyond the ordinary service inquiry is necessary.
The security arrangements provided by all the police forces which were involved in the royal visit were effective and successful and,

Canadian National Railways in spite of several demonstrations, at no time during the royal visit in any of the provinces that were visited by the Queen was there any attempt to molest Her Majesty, His Royal Highness or any member of the federal or provincial governments.
Neither I nor the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have received any complaints whatsoever regarding the security arrangements or the conduct of or action taken by any member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. On the contrary, the press and the public generally have commended the R.C.M.P. In these circumstances I am sure hon. members will agree that there is no occasion for me to direct an investigation.

subtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF RUN-THROUGHS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF RUN-THROUGHS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Melville, the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the pending changes at Sunday midnight, October 25, by the C.N.R. management which will establish run-throughs at the divisional points of Nakina and Wainwright, thus creating a great likelihood of a tie-up of the transcontinental line and tremendous hardship on the communities and railroaders affected.
In making the case for urgency I would point out that as you may have noted, Mr. Speaker, this matter was raised yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition, and several days before by the hon. member for Edmonton West. I have not made it an issue in terms of questions because delegations have come to Ottawa and we have been working through the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Transport on the assumption that this was the channel through which advice and representations should be passed to Mr. Gordon and the management of the C.N.R.
It is obvious that despite our representations and our efforts, Canadian National Railway officials have not seen fit to change their plans or to accept the request for postponement. The change is going to be introduced on Sunday night and, as I have expressed in the motion, there is every likelihood that this will create a situation that can tie up the transcontinental line of the C.N.R., and it may have even further ramifications. I do not

need to point out that such a situation has always been considered, in the Canadian political scene, as one of the most serious things that could happen.
I am making the point in addition, Mr. Speaker, that this move by Canadian National Railways, particularly as it affects Nakina and Wainwright, according to the contention of some of the men in the unions involved is a violation of an agreement entered into in 1926 between the Canadian National and the unions. This gives all the more reason for our feeling that a debate should take place on this matter, in order to bring to the attention of the Canadian National Railway and its president the need for, at the very least, a postponement of this decision for six weeks in view of the protests that may follow.
You will not mind if I point out, Mr. Speaker, that there is a motion for interim supply to follow which undoubtedly will give an opportunity to me and other members who are interested to speak on this problem. However, I want to put it to you that if, as I believe, this matter is of urgent importance, it deserves the significance of having the house accept this motion to give it the effect that I think it needs in order to put over to this crown agency, which has taken this action despite the representations that have been made, that to go ahead would involve consequences which I do not think I over estimate in presenting this motion to the house.

subtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF RUN-THROUGHS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
In seconding the motion moved by the hon. member for Port Arthur, Mr. Speaker, I am activated by the same concern for the railway employees which he indicated in sponsoring this motion. The situation regarding this proposed run-through operation is most controversial, and the railway employees feel that unilateral action has been taken by management to impose this change on the railway employees concerned. The railway employees feel that the urge by the railway companies to economize by instituting the new run-through system should not be acted upon without due consideration for its effect on the employees and their families, and on the economies of the local communities involved. Surely, with new railway legislation pending, there is a logical reason for a reappraisal of this whole program.
What the hon. member for Port Arthur has mentioned with regard to Wainwright and Nakina, which are isolated instances, will be

felt all over Canada and particularly in my own city of Melville, because there will be this change in pattern. It is for this reason, and because of the threatened deterioration of our system, that I urge some consideration be given to this matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllrailh (President of the Privy Council):
subtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF RUN-THROUGHS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while the matter raised by the hon. member is undoubtedly one of considerable importance, particularly in the two areas concerned, the point at issue here as I see it relates to the urgency of debate on this matter, and as to whether the matter is one coming under the administrative responsibility of the government. The purpose of rule 26, I respectfully submit, is to permit the discussion of a matter that is, by its nature, of such urgency that debate is required, taking precedence over all other opportunities in the house for discussing the matter and interrupting the ordinary business of the house for that purpose. It is a very extraordinary remedy and must be limited under the circumstances. In addition it is, of course, quite clear that it must be something related to the administrative responsibilities of the government.
As to the first point, the urgency of debate, 1 would draw Your Honour's attention to the fact that at the conclusion of the business of the house last night the item of business indicated for today was interim supply, when it is possible for an hon. member to raise a grievance against the government in the area of the government's administration. Therefore if the matter is indeed one that comes under the responsibility of the government administratively, it is properly discussable on interim supply which will come in a few minutes, I hope, when we reach orders of the day. Of course if it is not one within the administrative responsibility of the government then it is not something upon which a motion under standing order 26 can be raised.
I would like to direct Your Honour's attention to the first sentence in citation 100 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, which says:
The definite matter of urgent public importance for the discussion of which a member may ask leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 must involve the administrative responsibility of the government.
I want to point out that while this question of run-throughs may properly be of great concern to all hon. members, it is a matter for the administration of the Canadian National Railways, a statutory corporation created by statute of parliament; that parliament has divested the government of responsibility for the operation of the railway and has seen fit
Canadian National Railways to give that administrative responsibility to the Canadian National Railways by statute.
In support of that proposition I would refer Your Honour to an attempt made on March 13, 1961, by a former minister of transport to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26. On that occasion the matter had to do with a rather substantial proposed lay-off of men in the Montreal region. When the then hon. member for Laurier presented his motion he was advised by Mr. Speaker as follows, and I quote from page 2903 of Hansard for that date:
I shall be glad to hear the hon. member. I assume that it is a matter of importance, but the urgency that is involved is urgency of debate. I think I should like to hear the hon. member on the question of whether or not this is one of the administrative responsibilities of the ministry. It seems to me that the point may be well taken that it is a decision of the Canadian National Railways on its own authority.
That was very early in the attempt made by the hon. member to move the adjournment, and after considerable discussion, as recorded at page 2907 of Hansard, in giving his ruling Mr. Speaker went on to say:
The problem of their employment is, of course, an important matter to them at least and of significance to the Montreal area. However, parliament has given to the Canadian National Railways the responsibility for administering the railway and included in administration is the responsibility for all labour policy. It is true that parliament can change the legislation but it is not true, as I see it, that the government can intervene to direct Canadian National Railways to do something different.
At a later point he said:
It would be necessary for parliament to amend its Canadian National Railways legislation, if an enforceable decision is to be made or an effective remedy applied.
That may not appeal to all hon. members as a correct summary of the situation, but in addition to that point I think that lay-offs of this kind, whether isolated or part of a pattern, are a continuing problem of employees of the government owned railway which will be coming before the house from time to time when it is sitting, and should be dealt with on the occasions on which it is possible to debate the administrative policies of the Canadian National Railways and the control of these policies by parliament.
I therefore regretfully have to refuse the hon. member leave.
I suggest that the motion proposed today is directly parallel to the type of situation faced in 1961, and that leave should be refused for the reasons stated by the Speaker on that date.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF RUN-THROUGHS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words with respect to the question of urgency of debate. The President of the

Canadian National Railways Privy Council relied heavily on his contention that matters raised under standing order 26 must be matters within the administrative responsibility of the government. May I point out, however, that standing order 26 does not impose any such limitation; it is drawn to make possible discussion of questions of urgent public importance, and nowhere is discussion limited to matters which come under the administrative responsibility of the government. I would point out that only recently this house passed a provisional amendment to standing order 26, which implies that we have reviewed this standing order, and we did not feel it necessary to put in language of the kind the President of the Privy Council has just used.
The hon. gentleman quoted from citation 100 of Beauchesne's fourth edition. Of course he is a lawyer and I am not; therefore we have different views about precedents. But the citation he quoted is taken from a ruling given by Mr. Speaker Bowman in the House of Commons on May 22, 1935. All it amounted to was a ruling of the Speaker on that occasion. Anyone would agree, I think, that we should look at what was placed before Mr. Speaker Bowman on that occasion. In fact it was a motion to adjourn the house to discuss a certain matter, namely the presence of a large number of men from unemployment relief camps in the city of Vancouver. The contention put forward by those who opposed that motion-the contention accepted by Mr. Speaker Bowman-was that this was a matter which came within the responsibility of the provincial and municipal authorities.
I suggest the conclusion that it could not be brought before the house because it did not come within the administrative responsibility of the government was in the nature of an obiter dictum. All that Mr. Speaker said on that date was that this was a matter which came under the jurisdiction of the province of British Columbia or the city of Vancouver. I suggest, therefore, that it is improper to take that sentence out of Mr. Speaker Bowman's ruling and make it part of standing order 26, which it is not.
Standing order 26 provides for the discussion of a matter which is of urgent public importance. There is a limitation that it must be a matter on which debate is urgent. But we in parliament may feel that there are matters beyond those within direct governmental responsibility which should be discussed in this national forum and I submit, therefore, that this particular argument


of the President of the Privy Council falls to the ground.
I submit also that the hon. gentleman's contention that there is a parallel between what was proposed by Mr. Chevrier a few years ago and what is asked for today by my hon. friend from Port Arthur does not stand up. These are totally different matters. The concern then was the employment of a certain group of people. The concern now is a policy, the putting of which into effect could result in tying up the Canadian National main line right across this country. I suggest there is a difference, and that the case established for the urgency of debate is a prima facie case.
The only other point made by the President of the Privy Council is that interim supply has been listed as an item for debate today. My hon. friend from Port Arthur has already referred to this, and in my view he has a valid case in suggesting that this subject is in itself so important that it should be discussed now, not when anything else can intervene or at a time when it could only be sandwiched in among various speeches on other subjects on the motion for interim supply.
For these reasons I think Your Honour should recognize that the subject raised is one which meets the urgency of debate requirement.

subtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF RUN-THROUGHS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is just one matter I should like to add. The President of the Privy Council made the point that today we would be taking up interim supply. He also mentioned that the question before us was not one of government responsibility or one which should be discussed in parliament.

subtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF RUN-THROUGHS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: No, I did not say that.

subtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF RUN-THROUGHS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: The fallacy of this argument is that if we can discuss it on interim supply surely it is a matter which can be discussed in parliament. I suggest that this would bring it under standing order 26. The President of the Privy Council cannot have it both ways.

subtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF RUN-THROUGHS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a point here; I am sure the hon. member does not wish to misrepresent what I said. I did not for one moment suggest that this was a subject matter which could not be raised for debate in parliament. It is a subject matter which can be raised for debate in parliament. My point was that it is not a subject matter that warrants the usage of standing order 26, because standing order 26 can only

be made applicable to those matters which come under the direct administrative responsibility of the government. Therefore it must be debated in other areas of debate available in parliament. So the two points are quite separate. I never for one moment suggested that this was not a subject matter which should be debated in parliament.

subtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF RUN-THROUGHS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Just one word in reply to that. Standing order 26 refers to a definite matter of urgent public importance and I am sure does not limit itself in the way suggested by the President of the Privy Council. If it is a definite matter of urgent public importance, then it can be discussed under standing order 26. If it is not, then his argument about discussing it on interim supply today is not valid.

subtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF RUN-THROUGHS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Are there any other members who wish to help the Chair? If not, then first of all I should like to thank all hon. members who have contributed to the discussion and have been very helpful.
In my view there is no doubt about the importance here. Anything affecting the lives or the livelihood of seven or eight hundred people is certainly important. There is no doubt about the urgency of the matter, but in the view of Beauchesne in citation 100 (3), urgency means:
"Urgency" within this rule does not apply to the matter itself, but it means "urgency of debate", when the ordinary opportunities provided by the rules of the house do not permit the subject to be brought on early enough and public interest demands that discussion take place immediately
I may say in passing that in my view standing order 26 could apply to any public matter within the powers of the federal parliament.
As to the question of opportunity, Mr. Speaker Black on March 31, as reported at page 50 of the Journals for that day, said:
The reason for allowing such a motion-
-obviously under standing order 26.
-for the adjournment is to afford members an opportunity of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance which they could do in no other way-
So we have these two citations; that "urgency" means urgency of debate, and the decision of Mr. Speaker Black in 1931 concerning giving members an opportunity of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance which they could do in no other way.
In view of the fact that interim supply was announced last night and that there will be almost immediate opportunity to discuss this matter, it does seem to the Chair that
Inquiries of the Ministry there will be every opportunity of discussing this matter within a matter of minutes. Therefore I regret that, in my opinion, consent to adjourn the house under standing order 26 should not be granted at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I would now direct a question to the Acting Minister of Transport in connection with the action being taken by the Canadian National Railways. I asked him a question on this matter yesterday, and he said he would communicate with the C.N.R.

I do not know whether it is proper to refer to the Hansard blues, but as quickly as the blues could be obtained yesterday the actual text in connection with this matter was immediately communicated to the railway management. There was no instruction given, or

I have forgotten the word the right hon. gentleman used-
I think a good word would be "recommendation" from the minister.

Inquiries of the Ministry because I do not know whether that would be welcomed; I suspect it might not. In any event, I did not see fit to go beyond the authority granted to the minister under the legislation by taking this action. Perhaps I will have to leave my answer in that way.

I did not quite get the answer, Mr. Speaker, so I am rather uncertain about this. Was this suggestion met by silence on the part of the officials and the head of the C.N.R., or was it just disregarded? Because somehow the minister's answer seemed to die away.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, the answer died away because I do not know that it is proper for me to discuss the details of the conversations that have taken place. A great many discussions on this subject have gone on in the last week with the responsible officials in the railway company, and I do not think it is appropriate or proper for me to give the details of those conversations, other than to say this. Each representation, whether made in the house or made outside the house, by delegations either from communities or from unions, was communicated very promptly to the railway management, and there has been a great deal of responsible consideration given to this subject.

Then would the minister say, as to this question which was raised yesterday and which is of such importance, it having been placed before the president of the C.N.R., whether he gave an audible answer?
Mr. Speaker, the president of the C.N.R. is always audible.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the minister whether he actually got a negative reply, not to any persuasions he may have attempted but to representations. In other words, has the C.N.R. told him they are not going to postpone it but are going ahead?
Mr. Speaker, I have received no firm negative reply.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the minister whether he has consulted with the Minister of Labour and his officials about this particular problem, and whether they have brought forward any suggestions that might be useful in clearing up this situation.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I have consulted with him to a great extent on this


matter. We have had discussions about possible methods of dealing with the problems posed by the railwaymen in relation to the possible effect run-throughs might have.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a supplementary question. Would the minister inform the house whether he has received an unfirm negative reply from the railway officials?
No, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. Have the minister and the Minister of Labour been in touch with the employees concerned to ascertain whether we are going to have a stoppage on the transcontinental line next week?

Mr. Speaker, I do not think any of the employees have taken that position. In respect of all these disputes there is a great deal of talk, rumour and so on. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: RATE OF PAYMENT FOR EXTRA CHRISTMAS STAFF
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Postmaster General. In view of the questions raised by the Ontario department of labour, is the government considering paying Christmas postal staff less than the minimum Ontario wage and less than the proposed federal minimum wage?

subtopic: RATE OF PAYMENT FOR EXTRA CHRISTMAS STAFF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a brief answer would be no. Actually I think the hon. member's question arises out of a discussion that took place at the annual meeting of the Canadian postmasters association held here earlier this week. I took advantage of the presence of the postmasters in Ottawa to discuss certain things that were taking place, and I announced on that occasion that in semi-staff and revenue post offices a rate of 95 cents pei hour would be payable to Christmas help.
This is not less than the minimum rate There is legislation in the province of British Columbia fixing a minimum rate of $1, but for inexperienced help you can go as low as 85 cents. Similar legislation exists in Ontario, where the minimum rate is $1 but there is a leeway of 10 per cent for beginners or inexperienced help. The people, who are taken on in revenue post offices and semi-staff offices, not in the staff offices which are in the cities, are frequently high school students and others who are relatively in-

Inquiries of the Ministry experienced. Therefore in trying to establish what would be fair on a national basis we have picked 95 cents per hour, which is the highest provincial minimum established by statute in any of the 10 provinces.

subtopic: RATE OF PAYMENT FOR EXTRA CHRISTMAS STAFF
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Without wishing to be facetious, is this the spirit that the government is going to adopt in connection with its minimum wage of $1.25 an hour?

subtopic: RATE OF PAYMENT FOR EXTRA CHRISTMAS STAFF
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, it is in line with the spirit of the legislation. If the hon. member has read the bill introduced by the government, he will have seen that the objective of $1.25 is to be reached by July 1, 1966; and when we at this time move in the post office field from rates as low as 60 cents in some of the provinces to 95 cents, we are moving progressively in the direction envisaged by the proposed legislation.
Mr. Reid Scot! (Danforih): A supplementary question on this point. In view of the fact that most of these temporary workers are repeaters who have done the work from year to year for a considerable number of years, would the minister not agree that these are experienced people, and that the action of the department does violate the spirit of the Ontario minimum wage act?

subtopic: RATE OF PAYMENT FOR EXTRA CHRISTMAS STAFF
speechtext: With respect, Mr. Speaker, I will agree with the hon. gentleman that in cities of any size in Canada many of the Christmas helpers are experienced. In the case of the cities however, we do pay a minimum of $1 in all staff offices, as distinguished from semi-staff or revenue offices. The minimum is $1, and for heavy work the minimum is $1.25.

Mr. Chairman, the discussion of interim supply gives us an opportunity to accept the suggestion kindly put forward by the President of the Privy Council, the Acting Minister of Transport, to debate some of the matters concerning the management of Canadian National Railways and the implementation of some of the run-through systems which it is anticipated will be coming into effect in the next few days.
The hon. member for Port Arthur outlined the situation in a clear and concise manner, and other hon. members primarily interested in this problem include the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, myself, and the other hon.
Interim Supply
member who spoke earlier this morning. The problem involved is not new. It has been with us for several years, and the situation is likely to deteriorate before it becomes any better.
The Acting Minister of Transport is well aware of the situation. In the past he has been very co-operative, as a matter of fact sympathetic, and I am sure he has made every effort to bring the representations of the railway employees to the attention of management. Evidently, however, these representations have fallen on deaf ears, and we believe the new run-through system will be introduced in some areas very shortly.
At a time when the economy is fairly buoyant it is unfortunate that some areas of our country will suffer as a result of the proposals of Canadian National Railways. Trainmen have lived in these areas for many years, building up comfortable communities, and now it is possible that in the near future the population of these areas will be depleted as a result of the adoption of the run-through system. The basic idea of this system is that trainmen will spend longer time over longer distances performing their duties in running trains. This means that the turnaround points will be too far away for return trips, and will cut down on the time train crews are able to spend at home.
This is an inconvenience to the trainmen and their families, and I believe their feelings and the impact of this on their morale should be taken into consideration by management, which on many occasions has expressed its concern for the welfare of the workers. It must be evident that when employees are antagonistic to a system being imposed on them, their work will suffer.
The employees realize automation is inevitable and that management is willing to make certain concessions, but up to the present very little consideration has been given to the reasonable requests of railway-men who will be greatly inconvenienced by the new run-through system. Inevitably the population of some towns will be reduced, thus changing the economy of the areas around them.
Some consideration-and I do not mean just monetary consideration-must be given to employees who will be displaced. The run-through system may have some advantages. Possibly it will be more economical to the railway companies, but if the employees operating the trains are dissatisfied the railway operation in itself will suffer. Because of this we are asking the minister and the

Interim Supply
government to give consideration to some of the representations which have been made, and I urge the minister, his departmental officials and the railway management to sit down and once more discuss and analyse the situation in so far as it applies to railway employees.
I suppose I am fortunate in that the system is not to be introduced immediately in my area, but I understand it will be soon effective in other areas, and many areas will be adversely affected by it.
I feel the management of the C.N.R. has a responsibility to sit down again with the unions and try to work out a reasonable solution to this problem, which has been a festering sore for the last couple of years. Those members of the house who are more directly interested in these questions will be able to corroborate the statements I have made regarding the inconvenience which will be caused to these employees of the C.N.R. particularly, and a great deal of inconvenience will probably be caused to the travelling public as well. As the hon. member for Port Arthur has told us, time is running short, but I should like the minister to do everything in his power to see whether some solution can be reached to this urgent problem.

The step which the C.N.R. proposes to take on October 25 is another incident in what I have thought of all along as a long

and I am tempted to use the word "slimy"-series of incidents in which over the past decade the management of this railway has been following a policy amounting to "divide and rule". It has been a process of doing a little bit here and a little bit there; a process of changes and shifts, never coming out into the open with a clearcut plan. In the meantime they have managed to create an atmosphere in which you have a president of a railway who is probably as detested by a large group of people in Canada as anyone could possibly imagine.
It is not my purpose here to throw recriminations at Mr. Donald Gordon, but I wish to put this point before the committee. We are seeing the death arranged of communities in this country as a consequence of huge sums which this parliament has approved to allow the C.N.R. to make changes. We have approved the spending of billions of dollars to allow the C.N.R. to modernize, dieselize, introduce central traffic control and so on.
Members of this house who have served on the railway committee before which Mr. Gordon appears every year know that for a
[Mr. Ormiston.l
number of years I, in association with others in this house, have brought up this problem and tried to discuss the way in which the C.N.R. could make the adjustment. Only last July when Mr. Gordon was before the committee he was asked directly whether there were to be any more run-throughs in connection with the changes proposed as a result of dieselization. We also asked where these run-throughs would take place, if any were proposed.
We were fobbed off with the general answer that the C.N.R. was not yet in a position to reply. On September 15 it was announced to the local chairman at a divisional point that it had been decided to abandon the whole terminal of Nakina and run through. A parallel situation is that at Wainwright. There is no general plan. The C.N.R. refused to negotiate this question with the men's representatives in the unions at bargaining and contract time. Instead, they do a little here and a little there. They did it at Sioux Lookout; they did it at Belleville; they will never present a common problem.
I am sick of our approving expenditures for the Department of Labour to set up manpower consultative services, to study the effects of automation and how best to meet technological change. Here we have a prime example of technological change and its consequences. But are we prepared?
As the member most affected by the change to be introduced this Saturday, I have obviously played my hand incorrectly. This is a problem national in its scope. I thought the way to proceed was to make representations to the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Labour; to approach the problem quietly, with common sense and realism. Obviously an approach of this kind has not done any good. The Acting Minister of Transport by his remarks earlier today gave an indication that he sees himself, or his function, as simply a funnel or channel through which representations can be made. He regards himself as, in a sense, equivalent to a telegraph clerk or somebody who links up an intercom system. He did not seem to think he was in a position, in his relationship with the company, to add any force of persuasion at all.
In other words, in the representations we have made to the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Labour to the effect that there really is a good case for postponing this important move, we have not been able to carry conviction, or else the Acting Minister

of Transport feels he is in a strait-jacket because of the type of relationship which exists between the government and this crown agency and is unable to intervene in favour of this postponement.
One of the worst grey areas we have is this relationship between crown agencies and parliament. We know we are not administrators. We know we are not executives. But, somehow, the only way the spending of these agencies and the appointments to them can be legalized is by ourselves, acting in consort, doing something about it. We are on the scene; somehow or other we are in there. Yet we seem to be denied, perhaps properly so, any great influence; all we can do is talk about these things.
Well, talking is not very effective if one is talking to ministers who are not prepared to argue the case and take it to the head of the crown agency concerned, in this case the head of the C.N.R. I contend that the government should take a direct interest in this situation. For the first time a home terminal of the C.N.R. is being wiped out. A home terminal is a terminal from which railroaders operate.
I contend that this is probably an illegal action, and I am prepared at this time to say I will go into my area and work with the railroaders there in meeting this problem by what is possibly another illegal action, namely by a refusal to give service when the date comes. I may be penalized, and so may these men, for refusing to offer services on Saturday night. It may be held that a crime is being committed under the Criminal Code, but this is the situation to which long-suffering employees are brought in the absence of a constructive approach by management to grave situations such as this.
Knowing the minister personally and the interest he has taken in this-the good Lord knows the hon. gentleman has listened to me and I have listened to him in the last few weeks-it occurs to me he may think I am exaggerating, dealing in hyperbole because I am speaking in a public forum and appealing beyond it. But I would point out to the hon. gentleman how little is being asked for. The C.N.R. decided in mid-September to introduce changes on October 25 which will lead to the death of a town. It decided that on such short notice as this it would change traffic arrangements which have been in effect for generations. Is it not reasonable to ask for a postponement?
We have before the house at the present time amendments to the Railway Act. We have all been told about the scope of this

legislation based on the deliberations of a royal commission. Included in it are provisions dealing with section 182 of the Railway Act which has been a matter of contention for a decade. I think the minister likes technical points, so I would mention this. The Railway Act is before the house for amendment. It is the right of everyone to move amendments, and I have already indicated that I am going to offer an amendment to section 182 of the act which, if accepted by the house, will have the effect of bringing situations such as those existing in Nakina or Wainwright under the purview of the act. Among the recommendations made by the railway committee, which is the same committee which will be handling the Railway Act, there was a strong recommendation that this kind of situation be met by a change in legislation. I wonder how many hon. members noticed, Mr. Chairman, that recently the Canadian Pacific Railway announced that it would suspend passenger operations on its day-liner service between Peterborough and Toronto. Public opinion geared the newspapers to take the matter up, members of parliament were contacted, representations were made and the acting minister expressed concern. A few days ago, before it was announced in the house the Canadian Pacific Railway indicated that it was not going to go ahead with the withdrawal of this passenger service at this time. I mention that as an indication that there is nothing fundamental about postponing something. It is a very simple request.
Yet Canadian National Railways have given no information at all about this matter. I have information that it has alerted its officials, trainmasters and so on, so that in

the event there is a withdrawal of service the men who ordinarily move the transcontinental trains will be ready to move over for a period while the squeeze is put on the men. This information I have is reinforced by the fact that the C.N.R. has wired the people of Nakina to the effect that the offer made a couple of weeks ago-belatedly-to buy their homes still holds, which is surely an indication that there is some kind of conscience in this matter. Why would this offer be repeated if it was turned down by the men and by the community? It has been repeated because the company feels that this will be a sort of oyster for someone to reach for as the men begin to worry and to fear the power of this company if it does withdraw this service.
This is a power game, and the people who are under the power of this company are out along the periphery in small towns along the system without the resources of communications media which can really build up their case as the Peterborough case was built up. They do not have a couple of columnists in Toronto who were riding this dayliner and who built up the case in the newspapers. These people are exposed to the power of the major employer of the area, an employer who, in the main, has indicated that in matters like this it is prepared to be ruthless.
I have never liked the contention that the Minister of Transport is just a funnel through which you can drop something and it will get to the president of the Canadian National Railways. On the other hand, I am not one who believes that the Minister of Transport is at all times second guessing the president of the Canadian National Railways. Nevertheless we have to assume there is a relationship somewhere between the funnel and the Charlie McCarthy kind of act.
I suggest that the difference here is exposed in specific situations. Normally you leave the Canadian National Railways free from advice on minor matters, but when something major brews up it seems to me you have to have consultation and a rather full explanation of policy. One of the regrettable things, despite the questions which have been asked in the house, is that the minister has come into this place and given us no information at all on the Canadian National point of view. He could not even transmit a firm negative today. In other words the matter is still up in the air.
The situation roughly is this. Canadian National Railways, as a result of great expenditure, has to make changes in its arrangements. It feels it has to do this. It has not worked out any system of doing this. A lot of people say, why is it that Canadian National is in the van? Why is it that Donald Gordon always carries the ball and is the aggressor? Why is it not the Canadian Pacific Railway, the private enterprise outfit, which is in this position?
I will tell you why, Mr. Chairman, and it is very simple. The unions working under the Canadian Pacific Railway have protection because they have no big seniority districts, and no changes can be made in the working conditions of the contracts which affect them in any single one of the terminals. But the situation is different with the Canadian National. It is organized-and this has been very useful to the company over the years-in big seniority districts. In this way it can make a change which will wipe out Nakina and its railwaymen and will bump along all the way down through Capreol to Toronto, and so on, and there is no way the men can come at this as the railway interprets it.
There is an agreement in existence. There is a 1926 Montreal agreement entered into between the brotherhood of locomotive firemen and enginemen and the brotherhood of locomotive engineers and the C.N.R. Section 9 of that Montreal agreement sets out that no changes will be made in the set-up regarding home terminals without prior conference, arrangement and negotiation between the management and the unions. This agreement can only be rescinded on 30 days' notice. As far as I know this agreement still exists and is still in effect. The railway does not want to talk about it. It does not even want to give notice of rescission, because it knows that something will blow up. This brings a very large issue into some kind of arrangement for negotiation.
I do not think the Minister of Transport has really realized the way the C.N.R. has moved on this whole question of technological change. It has never given us any over-all policy. What they are doing in Wainwright is hitting the trainmen over the head with the club and leaving the firemen and engineers alone. At Nakina the situation is the opposite. They haggle and nip a piece off here and a piece off there and never give the railway-men an opportunity of seeing what is the over-all plan or structure. I suppose that is good labour relations. It is good labour relafMr. Fisher.]

tions on the basis that the arrangement between management and labour is a war of some kind and that it is good to outsmart the opposition, but it really is not good enough in a situation where we have technological change of such scope.
What will this do to the town of Nakina; and it will bump others along the way? This is a town of 800 people. Approximately half of them are railroaders and dependants. In two years all will be gone. What are the consequences for a town which has a school, roads into it, a Legion and churches? In effect it means the end of the town. The town may have other prospects because of very large iron resources which happen to be nearby, but in effect it is a town created by Canadian National Railways, created by Sir Henry Thornton and killed by Donald Gordon. Surely there is a greater responsibility here than just making a decision like this. Nevertheless Mr. Gordon has decided to do it; and make no mistake about it, Mr. Chairman, this decision was not reached at the local level; this decision has come right out of Montreal. We are going to begin the ending of this town's existence. And this is only the first one. Biggar will be next. Wainwright is under the gun this time, of course.
Where is a policy to meet this situation? Are the Minister of Transport and his colleague the Minister of Labour going to keep on insisting that they can only transmit representations which are made, that they have no responsibility and that there is no onus on them to see that a better plan is forthcoming? This may be the new co-operative federalism, I do not know, but it certainly offers very little and makes hypocrisy of a great deal many of us have said here during our consideration of the estimates of the Department of Labour. I thought we were going to have some kind of reasoning and planning in this regard. The Minister of Labour is touting his doctrine of economic planning around the country, and we have created the new Department of Industry to do something about this whole question of planning and developing industry and regional co-ordination. I'll bet the Minister of Labour has never even heard of Nakina and Wainwright.
And couldn't care less.

That may be his Goldwater phase, but I do not know about that.
My point is that we have all these agencies and we have talked about our responsibilities in this situation, but when we get down to 20220-594

Mr. Chairman, as I conclude my contribution to this debate I should like to refer to the seriousness of the political aspect of this situation. The thing that has galled me about the Liberal party ever since I was a small boy is their damnable arrogance as a total crew. I have always felt that Donald Gordon is sort of a perfect administrative instrument for that kind of arrogance that has been associated with the Liberal party and its record. It seems to me that one of the most galling things that can happen is for a minister of the crown, and the government, to assume that questions such as the one to which I have referred should be left to the administrative competence and decision of these crown agencies. That seems to me to be the core of Liberal party doctrine. Their doctrine seems to be that these questions should be left to be answered by those who know best, in this case the president of the C.N.R.
Mr. Chairman, we all know what happened to parliament under the Liberal regime up to 1957. It was falling away, and everything was being left to a group of administrative geniuses who supposedly knew how to do things. I want to inform the Acting Minister

Interim Supply
of Transport, much as I have appreciated all the assistance he has given in the last week or two, that I cannot help but read into the general reaction of the government the feeling that they assume they are really a funnel through which representations pass. I have noticed that in almost every case. That is an example of the existence of that same old Liberal arrogance.
Mr. Chairman, there is a final irony to this whole situation. Most railroaders along the Canadian National Railways tend to vote Liberal. This is a long tradition which goes back to the ability of Mackenzie King to settle railway strikes at the time of the first world war. This tradition is related to the fact that this region of Canada was settled during a Liberal administration many years ago, and the railroaders have tended to look at that party with kindness. The final irony is that one of the hardest things I have had to do, as have the Conservatives, has been to convince these men that all their faith placed in the Liberal party for so many years has been proven repeatedly during the last generation to be absolute nonsense.
I do not want to dot the "i" too much in this regard, but I will always remember the people of Redditt, Kenora and Sioux Lookout coming to Ottawa in conection with the same kind of problem a few years ago, on which occasion they discovered that the Liberal representative for Kenora had difficulty even arranging a meeting for them, let alone carrying their case.
I can only come to the conclusion that one of the features of this whole situation is that we have a government which refuses to even go to the trouble of asking, with some firmness, that the railway officials postpone this decision for six or eight weeks, or until this parliament can consider appropriate legislation. I do not think that in these circumstances I can do anything else than carry back to my area, or anywhere else I go in the country, the feeling that we have here an indifferent regime with that kind of arrogance I have come to identify with the Liberal party. All I can do is say how much I regret that this is my conclusion about the attitude of this government regarding a problem which I feel should be aside and apart from any partisanship or politicking.

Mr. Chairman, when this item was called I was in the process of rising in my place for the purpose of making it clear that the usual undertaking was being given in connection with this interim supply motion, 
that the passing of interim supply would not prejudice the position of hon. members. I want to make it clear now that this committee can assume that that undertaking has been given.
The question raised by the hon. member for Melville is an important one, and I think he presented an objective statement to this house about a problem which is of great concern to the House of Commons and to parliament generally. He referred to the difficult consequences of automation and its effect upon employees who will be dislocated because of changing procedures. He also mentioned the possible detrimental effect on communities involved.
I must contrast his method of presentation with that of the hon. member for Port Arthur, who raised two main points. Undoubtedly they are closely related, but I think he unnecessarily confused the two. He referred to the important problem of the dislocation of railway employees and the consequential effect on communities. He referred also to the immediate local difficulties at Nakina and related communities.
The hon. member for Port Arthur saw fit to commence his presentation by using some language with which I cannot associate myself. I do want to point out to the committee, though, that in my view at least this is not the method to approach a difficult problem like this if any appropriate solution is to be reached. It will be recalled that he started his remarks by referring to the management of Canadian National Railways as slimy.

Just a minute. On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I intended to say and believe I said that there was a long history of a slimy trail in management-labour relations on the C.N.R. There is some difference.

Mr. Chairman, I completely accept the hon. member's explanation of the difference, but I will let the record speak for itself. I respectfully suggest this is not the way to bring the facts before the committee, but that is his responsibility and not mine. I want to dissociate myself publicly from that kind of argument.
He then moved on in the next sentence or two to make a personal reference to the president. He did not say that his actions were in any way wrong, but he made a personal reference by speaking about the extent to which he said the president was

personally detested. Then he moved on to the acting minister and chose to refer to him as the equivalent of a telegraph operator. His opinion of the acting minister is, I am sure, of no concern to the committee. It certainly does not concern me in the least, because I think hon. members will make their own assessment in regard to these matters and I am content to leave it there. He referred later to the acting minister as a Charlie McCarthy.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, if the minister wants to take this line I hope he will listen a bit. What I suggested was that it seemed to me there were two possibilities for a minister of transport, and one to be more or less a funnel or telegraph operator or a Charlie McCarthy, the kind of arrangement where he would be standing at the shoulder of the president of the C.N.R. I do not mind the minister making these remarks, but I do not think he should get that far away from what I said.

If I may continue, Mr. Chairman, I did the hon. member the courtesy of not interrupting him at any point. Perhaps it is clear now that I should have done so as he went along, but in any event I did not. He then concluded his argument with a reference to the damnable arrogance of the Liberal party and proceeded to identify the president of the C.N.R. as the chosen instrument-I think that is the term he used- for expressing that attitude.
I want to invite the committee's attention to the fact that I think it would be quite impossible to find any arrogance or damnable arrogance in the treatment of this subject since it arose, and in my opinion the answers to questions on the orders of the day in the last number of days should have indicated that there is nothing but great concern over this matter.

tern of railway divisional points approximately 125 miles apart was set up in the days of the coal burning engines. It has been thought fit by management to seek to change that system with the advent of diesel engines involving different methods of servicing and different requirements inherent in the technological improvements in the building of engines for hauling trains. I do not want to divert into a discussion of the matter at the moment, but I suppose it will be generally granted that there must be necessary changes arising from this development. Indeed, changes are desirable if the users of the railway services are to be properly served by this transportation medium.
Therefore the matter is one of making sure that the changes are brought about in a way that is not harmful but rather is beneficial to all the interests concerned, which in the final analysis really means the public through-: out the country, rather than merely dealing with the problem from the point of view that there must be no change, period, and that anything that was established in the past must be left completely untouched. I would hope that would be common ground.
With regard to Nakina, when the initiation of the run-throughs was announced it was made clear by the railway company that it was proposed to introduce the run-throughs over a period of two years. That was made very clear, and it has always been clear. It was also made clear that the details of the method of introducing and bringing about the run-throughs were open for discussion. That was repeatedly made clear by the railway, management both to the community representatives with whom they discussed this matter and to the railwaymen concerned. Again, because the situation did not seem to be fully appreciated, it was made clear to the men by letter of October 8 in the proper way through the appropriate union authorities. It was also requested in the letter that anyone who wished to make any proposals on this matter should put them forward.
I am only the acting minister. I regret that the minister is absent, although we are looking forward to his return in a very few days. However, when I first learned of the proposition that had been made by management to the men and to the community, and sensed from the delegation who came to see me that it had not been properly appreciated, I took the liberty of reiterating it to the delegation in, I think, rather clear fashion. This has always been the position of management, and so far no proposals or suggestions on this

point have been made. No advantage has been taken of the proposition put forward by the railway, either by the men or the community.
There is another facet about which I should speak. Very early in the course of events, as this difficulty was building up, the railway management put forward another proposition. It was that they would buy the homes of employees if these employees were moving from the town of Nakina. A method of valuation was established involving three valuators who would fix prices. One valuator was to be from the railway, one from the owners' group and an independent valuator was to be chosen by the other two. Hon. members will appreciate that the railway was going quite a long way, in that such a proposition is quite new. They put forward that proposition because of the particular nature or extent of the dependence of Nakina on the railway, and the history of the development of the town in relation to the railway. This has two consequences; it saves the individuals employed from any economic loss if they choose to move, and it also means that the community continues to receive its taxes on those houses.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose for the noon adjournment I had been explaining the proposal put forward by the management of the Canadian National Railways concerning the proposed run-through at Nakina. I indicated that the management had dealt with the individual employees of the railway company at Nakina, and had put forward a scheme for purchasing the homes of any of the employees who would wish to move from Nakina consequent upon the implementation of the run-through. Further, I indicated the basis of valuation, and said the company had also dealt with employees individually on arrangements regarding moving expenses.
I then went on to state that the company had indicated it was prepared to consider or discuss any counter-proposals which the men might have to advance, and that the plans for implementing the run-through were completely flexible, subject to one condition which apparently I did not mention before one o'clock, that the program of implementing the

run-through be completed in two years, that is by the latter part of 1966.
I also indicated that the significance of these proposals and the invitation to put forward counter-proposals had not, in my view, been fully appreciated, and when I sensed this I made the point clear to the representatives of the community who attended as a delegation in Ottawa. The railway management also made this clear in a letter sent to the appropriate union officials involved, but as yet no counter-proposals have been made.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: A counter-proposal with regard to what?
A counter-proposal regarding the timing and the method of implementing the run-throughs; and there was one condition, namely that the run-throughs be fully implemented by two years from now.
Surely the minister would acknowledge that a request was made for a six weeks postponement so that the matter could be discussed more fully?

I am coming to that point as I develop my remarks. No counter-proposal has yet been received in the context in which I have explained the invitation, and I think I have tried to make my remarks as accurate and precise as possible on this point. However, after the delegation attended in Ottawa last Friday, some time early this week a request was received from the community representatives asking for a postponement of the starting date of the implementation of the program,
A start was to be made on the program on October 25, just two days from now, but the community's request was limited to delaying the start of the program, and carried with it a plea that the whole matter be discussed. It did not carry with it any acquiescence in the whole program being implemented at the end of two years. Indeed the delegation made it quite clear they were completely opposed to the run-through, and that is where the matter stands now.
There are some other aspects of this matter on which I would like to speak for a moment or two. The hon. member for Port Arthur indicated to the committee-and I wish to draw the hon. member's attention specifically to this, so that I may not be accused of misinterpreting his remarks-that the action taken by the railway was probably, in his view, an illegal action, and he went on to tell the committee he would go into this area

and work with the railroaders there in meeting this problem by what would, possibly, be another illegal action, namely by a refusal to give service when the date comes. He went on to say that he might be penalized, and so might the men, for refusing to offer services on Saturday night and that it might be held a crime was being committed under the Criminal Code. Nevertheless, he observed, this was the situation to which long-suffering employees had been brought in the absence of a constructive approach by management to grave situations such as this.
I think I have accurately repeated what the hon. member said. I want now to draw his attention to this. He told us that in this difficult situation the approach by management had not been constructive. That is a legitimate argument and I have no objection whatever to such an argument being put forward. But here we have a member of the House of Commons indicating that he proposes to violate the law, and I want to ask him: What kind of constructive action is that? The people of this country have a representative in parliament who says he intends to act illegally and wilfully to break the law of this country. In other words he is not willing to use the methods which are open to him under the law but is asserting he will break the law. I would ask the hon. member to consider very carefully whether this is a helpful or constructive attitude to take in what is admittedly a difficult situation. Is this the kind of action which is likely to be helpful in bringing about a suitable solution to a problem of labour-management relations? Surely this is not the kind of example which should be given to employees of any company or to citizens of the country generally. I invite the hon. member to consider further what he said on this point and what his action should be.

Would the minister permit a question? I wonder if the hon. gentleman would consider suggesting to the C.N.R. that the company should live up to the spirit of section 182 of the Railway Act, which it has consistently violated over the years.
I do not agree that the railways have consistently, over the years, violated section 182 of the Railway Act. But I will deal with the points raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur-

They have violated the law in the province of Quebec, with their trucking system, and they are now before the
Interim Supply
courts; yet they continue their operations. The minister knows that.

I will deal with points arising out of section 182 of the Railway Act in a few moments to the extent I think it is proper to do so during a debate on interim supply. In any event, turning now to the Nakina aspect of this matter arising from the technological changes due to automation and so on, it would seem to me that this aspect is a matter for the management of the railroad-that this is something relating wholly to the operations of the company. It would seem that in dealings with particular employees-I have in mind now the more restricted aspect of the problem as it immediately affects the situation at Nakina-the railways, or management, have made responsible offers to the men-some might say they were generous-and that in this narrower aspect they have shown a most considerate attitude toward the human element. Having said this, I agree there is a larger aspect of the whole matter which was raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur, and I sought at the outset of my remarks to indicate that in my view there are two closely related, though none the less separate questions raised in his argument, one of them being the whole question of the consequences of automation as it affects railroad employees and communities consequent upon the implementation of run-throughs by railways. In this context the hon. member raised the possibility of amending section 182 of the Railway Act and he developed his argument by suggesting other means of dealing with this problem. This is a much larger and, I agree, a most important question. For my part I do not know whether it is appropriate for me in a debate on interim supply to seek to outline precisely what should be done with regard to this question. But I would point out to the committee that the Department of Labour has set up an advisory committee on technological changes composed of representatives of government and of labour and management, a committee which is now considering this type of problem in its broader aspect, and it must surely be apparent to all members that the subject matter which the hon. member had in mind is being dealt with.
There are several arguments one could make with regard to the precise method which might best be used for dealing with this problem. It has been suggested it should be dealt with under section 182 of the Railway Act. I must frankly say I am convinced this is not the best possible way of dealing with

Interim Supply
it. Another suggestion is that general legislation should be enacted to deal with the whole question. Just how this would be done, I do not know. Another school of thought takes the view that this is a subject for negotiation and coverage by union agreements. In any event it is apparent one could develop various arguments about which method of dealing with this problem would be the most suitable. Since I am neither the Minister of Transport, who is directly responsible for railway matters, nor the Minister of Labour, I would consider it inappropriate, in an interim supply debate, to argue-and indeed I have some doubt at the moment as to my competence to argue-as to precisely which method should be followed.
It is clear-however-that the government is concerned with this problem and that a government advisory committee within one of the departments is dealing with it. I believe it is an able committee and it might well be it should concern itself more directly with this particular problem. I know it will be unsatisfactory to many hon. members if I say that the immediate aspect of the implementation of the run-through policy at Nakina is a matter for the management of the railway. I appreciate that this will be quite unsatisfactory. Yet I believe it would be less than fair to hon. members if I were to indicate otherwise.
That is the fact as I believe it to be. Goodness knows all concerned, notwithstanding the tremendous burden there is on the railways because of the restrictions we have placed on them, will agree they must be kept efficient. I believe all hon. members will agree that on aspects which are purely for management in the internal operations of the railways it is desirable that members do not interfere.
Unsatisfactory as that answer may appear superficially to be, I believe it is important that it be asserted, but at the same time that a solution be sought to the larger, major question. I assure hon. members that this subject matter has been receiving very careful consideration, although perhaps over too short a period of time. Every aspect of the matter debated today of direct concern to the railways was communicated immediately i to them on every occasion. The other larger question is, of course, receiving continuing attention, as its nature warrants that it must.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks I should like to make in connection with this important matter involving, as it does, the question of automation and tech-

nological advances. We cannot, of course, go into a lot of detail in this regard on a debate such as this, but it does seem to me that technological advances and automation are nothing new. However, government policy, particularly at the federal level, must be geared to take care of the circumstances that arise out of these technological changes and automation, and it seems to me we are lagging far behind in this regard.
I do not think we should be afraid of technological advances and automation. As a matter of fact we should welcome anything which will raise the standard of living of all our peoples. I am reminded of the speech made by the Minister of Labour, which was quite fully covered on a television program last night, in which he regretted that in many parts of Canada today people are in abject poverty. Here we find we are moving into a situation which will add to the distress of the people in the areas concerned because we have failed to go ahead with our plans to take care of situations which arise owing to technological advances and automation.
To the people who are affected this is a very serious matter. The minister has said that the railway company has agreed to buy the homes of these individuals. They might buy the houses of the individuals but they cannot buy the homes, because a home is more than just a place to live in. The association of a community is part of home life, and there is more to that than just buying the house of an individual or buying his assets. Surely this step should only take place under certain conditions, and there are a lot of ways in which this disagreeable move can be made less agonizing if the proper steps at the proper time are taken.
According to the minister, the over-all plan is to get these changes through by 1966. It would seem to me that with the moves which have been made to get some action on section 182 of the Railway Act over the years, certainly somebody has slipped up somewhere when there comes to light a situation where plans have been made to eliminate by 1966 many of these small places through action taken by the railways. I am one of those people who believe that we should never fear change or be afraid to move along; but at the same time where human beings and families are involved I think we should certainly take a much more serious look at the implications of such moves.
At this point I think I should say that I believe that a postponement of the railway's

plan is absolutely necessary. I think we must allow for further consideration of this particular case. There is no doubt at all in my mind that for the efficiency of the railroad these changes are good and I think they must come. It has been the practice of the railways over the years to make these changes at the same time as they make major changes in their time tables. Having this in mind it seems to me that there will be no great hardship in the offing either to the railroad or to anyone else if this proposed change was left over until next spring when the time tables of the railway companies are changed again. There are summer and winter schedules, and as I say it has been the practice of the railway companies to make most of their changes at the same time as they make the change from summer to winter schedules or winter to summer schedules.
I believe the management of the railway could easily bring about a discussion of this matter, such as we are having in this committee today, so as to bring the whole business into focus. I can understand that a businessman who is running a railway and having to deal with government, with parliament and with population, would demand that drastic action be taken where there is a lack of initiative on the part of the government. I suggest to hon. members that the railway company has been forced into taking this drastic action in order to focus attention on the problem. Certainly we have not received from the government any indication that the action necessary to forestall the inconvenience and hardship which is going to be caused the people affected will be taken. Therefore I would urge the government to take a very serious and hard look at this whole situation, to do what they can to influence the railways to postpone the action contemplated in these run-throughs and to find some real solution to the problem.
The minister says he is not certain whether section 182 should be changed. I agree that there are other types of business, occupations and operations facing the same problem with which we are confronted here, and perhaps section 182 of the Railway Act is not the place to make this sort of change. If this is not the place to make the changes let us move on and make changes where they should be made, so that this kind of thing can be taken care of whether it be in respect of mining, farming in dried out areas or railways and other services. Let us move in a direction which will lead to some permanent
