solution to the problem with which we are faced in respect of displaced persons as a result of automation and technological advances.

Mr. Chairman, while the minister was speaking before our luncheon adjournment he took exception to some interjections I made in his speech and in the speech of the hon. member for Port Arthur. Having heard the minister speak since lunch time I not only have no apology to make, but I wish my interjections had been made in a stronger vein.
I do not know why the minister took exception to the fact the hon. member for Port Arthur put the responsibility for what is taking place at Nakina directly on the shoulders of the president of the C.N.R. and the government. Surely the president of the C.N.R. must accept responsibility for everything the C.N.R. has done, whether he, a vice president or an official at Nakina issued the orders. Surely the president is responsible for the actions taken by the C.N.R., whether they are right or wrong. Certainly the hon. member for Port Arthur need not feel that he should explain or apologize for what he said about Mr. Gordon. If the actions contemplated by the C.N.R. this week end are wrong in principle and will adversely affect the people of Nakina, surely the government must accept responsibility.
We are not discussing this issue only because of the adverse effects it will have on a small town in northwestern Ontario, in spite of the fact that the town will be almost wiped out. We are discussing this situation because it is the first change of a series which undoubtedly the C.N.R. contemplate.
Let me make it clear that neither I, any other member of this party, nor perhaps any member of this house, objects to the C.N.R.'s actions and necessary steps to make it as efficient as possible, enabling it to move passenger and freight traffic as economically as possible to compete with other forms of transportation. On the other hand, we do have a right to expect the government and the C.N.R. to give some thought to the costs involved. Included in those costs must be considered the disruption of the lives of the many people who are not being asked to sacrifice only a few hundreds or thousands of dollars, but their whole way of life.
For the past two or three years members of the present government have been travelling from one end of Canada to the other talking about the importance of planning,

Interim Supply
and suggesting that this country will not develop in full the use of its material and manpower resources without intelligent planning. The Minister of Labour was in Hamilton last night talking about the benefits of automation, and what automation could do for Canada if we only had the intelligence to use it properly. Not so many months ago the Minister of Forestry, at a conference in Toronto, attended by a number of members of parliament, referred to the benefits of planning and direction by the federal government in co-operation with provincial and municipal governments. Indeed that minister went so far as to refer to himself, and this is often considered to be a dirty word, as a socialist. I do not know how he fits in with the ideas expressed by the Minister of Transport, or that great exponent of free enterprise, the Minister of Industry. That is the kind of talk regarding planning we have heard from one end of Canada to the other.
The present situation provides a concrete test, rather than a test of theory, as far as efficiency of operation is concerned. Surely the C.N.R. is not a company that can exercise the rights of free enterprise, to run its business in any way it sees fit which will be only to the greatest advantage of its shareholders. This is a company owned and operated by and for the people of Canada. This company was not built to make money, but was built to meet a political situation in Canada, to provide coast to coast transportation. This is a company which has received and continues to receive massive subsidies from the people of Canada. These subsidies run in the neighbourhood of hundreds of millions of dollars. Every year this company comes to the parliament of Canada asking for millions of dollars to help meet its deficits. If we pass the railway legislation proposed ostensibly to implement the recommendations of the MacPherson report this company will receive further hundreds of millions of dollars in subsidies.
This company has decided that in order to be more efficient the workers of a small town in northwestern Ontario will have to be moved. What is this great planning about which the acting minister spoke so glowingly today? The company has indicated that it is willing to make contributions toward the purchase of the homes to be vacated by these people. I do not think the hon. member for Port Arthur was scathing enough in his remarks about the Liberal party, if the pending action by the C.N.R. is an example of its thinking on planning.

The provincial department of education recently built a high school in the area of Nakina at a substantial cost, with the understanding that a number of students from Nakina would attend that school. The provincial government spent a substantial amount of money to build a paved highway into Nakina five or six years ago. All that money will be going down the drain because these services will be completely useless with the run-throughs which the C.N.R. has ordered go into effect next week end. That town will virtually become a ghost town.
All these facts have been ignored by the acting minister. I should not expect anything more because he is typical of the do nothing, stand pat, business as usual Liberals who really run the show. Why are we concerned in this regard? We are concerned because we realize this is only the first step. I had a telephone conversation with an individual in Winnipeg last evening as a result of which I am sure that the step to be taken at Nakina this week end is only a first step in a program of this kind. In the very near future major changes affecting the Winnipeg area will take place. Many workers in the past six years have been shifted from Sioux Lookout and Redditt to Winnipeg. Soon they will be shifted again from Winnipeg to areas further west, if the projected plans of the C.P.R. in respect of run-throughs are carried out. These individuals, who in the last six years were shifted from western Ontario to Winnipeg, will again have to move from Winnipeg to somewhere in Saskatchewan and work on services from Saskatchewan back to Winnipeg. I do not know whether the C.N.R. will think them important enough to compensate them for their homes in Winnipeg. Probably they will not, because this is the first time they have ever made such an offer and I am sure they did not do so voluntarily, or with very good grace. So, Mr. Chairman, for the minister to say that this is not a very important or big matter is for him simply to beg the issue.
The minister said that he advised the railway unions and these people to make a counter-proposal. How ridiculous can you be, Mr. Chairman? This problem cannot be solved in Nakina or Wainwright. Railway workers from one end of Canada to the other are concerned and upset because they know what has happened in the last 15 years and they know that the tremendous changes which have taken place are going to continue. You cannot expect the people in Nakina or Wainwright or their local or national unions to

work out a plan to apply to only these two places.
Surely if the government really believes in what it has said about planning so eloquently, so often and in so many places, the government ought to be urging, in fact directing the management of the C.N.R. not simply to tell the railway workers and their unions what is going to happen on Sunday in Nakina and Wainwright but to tell them what their plans are for the next five or ten years. Let railway management work out a national plan in co-operation with the railway workers and their unions.
I suggest to members of the committee there is not a single railway worker or a single railway union that does not know about and agree with the idea that the railways have to be modernized and have to change their methods of operation, but the workers do not want to carry the whole burden and they should not be expected to do so. It behooves the management of the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. as well as the government of Canada to work out plans for an orderly transition.
The acting minister says today, as the Minister of Transport said on September 14 when we discussed his estimates for one day, that the department is not satisfied that section 182 of the Railway Act is the proper method by which to protect the rights of the railway workers. The railway workers and their unions are not very concerned about what section of the Railway Act is used, whether it is section 182 or another section or whether entirely new legislation is adopted, but they are tired of the excuses that have been made year by year by railway management and by the government. They want action.
The railway workers are not opposed to the principles and recommendations of the MacPherson report. They are not opposed to reorganization and rationalization of the railways. They are not opposed to the railways being put into a position where they will be able to compete fairly with all other methods of transportation. But they are fed up with the idea prevalent in railway management, which I must say it seemed to me the acting minister expounded very well for railway management, that everything must be done to modernize and rationalize the railways, but nothing can be done to protect the rights of the railway workers, to make sure that there is an orderly transition and that people who have worked for the railway for 10, 15
Interim Supply
or 20 years are not thrown on the scrap heap.
I am not going to prolong the debate at this time. However, if the government persists in ignoring and sloughing off the railway workers with double talk when they ask for guarantees in the proposed railway legislation so that they will not be treated in the future as they have been in the past, if the government persists in saying that section 182 is not the right section but they do not know what is, if the government says again what the Minister of Transport said to me on September 14, that the only way this matter can be handled is in the over-all method of handling the problem of automation through setting up a technical committee in the Department of Labour with really no power to do anything, then I want to warn the acting minister right now that it will be a long, long time before the proposed railway legislation will pass, if it ever does. The government is going to have to do a great deal better than it has or it will not get the co-operation of the house in passing that legislation.

Mr. Chairman, I must say I listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Melville regarding run-throughs and the many people who will be affected. I also listened with interest to the hon. member for Port Arthur who covered the subject extensively. One thing that gives me great concern is Bill No. C-120 and the question of rail line abandonment. In the railway committee I put questions to the president of the Canadian National Railways about this matter. I think it is most unjust for the C.N.R. to talk about rail line abandonment before it has fulfilled its obligations.
I remember quite well when the Shell-brook-Turtleford line was constructed and how the department of colonization of the C.N.R. went into the area and encouraged homesteaders to settle there and develop the country. I have seen how Canadian National Railways has fallen down on its part of the bargain over the years by never completing this line. It now claims that the line does not pay, but the fact is it has not lived up to its responsibility to complete the gap from Frenchman Butte to Heinsburg, Alberta. It should keep in mind those people who have spent the greater part of their lives in developing this area because the fact is that it is the mismanagement of the Canadian National which has made it impossible for the line to be a paying one, simply because

Interim Supply
of the failure to complete the gap of 38 miles. If this were done we would have a main route that would serve northern Alberta including the salt mines at Heinsburg. There would be a direct run from Winnipeg through Prince Albert and North Battleford and the line could very easily be made to pay. But the C.N.R. has this line on its list for abandonment. In talking about abandonment it is betraying those people who went in there and developed that region. The C.N.R. has not lived up to its part of the bargain. If it had done so the line would have paid but it has failed to fill this gap of 38 miles across level country.
If the C.N.R. would take stock of its own failures with regard to some of the lines it is talking about abandoning, I think there would be a different feeling in western Canada. The people in this area are very much concerned because they settled there, established homes, built up fine farms and raised their families. But now they find they are going to be without a rail line of any kind and in many cases they will be 75 to 100 miles away from the nearest rail point. The people of western Canada are very much concerned about these things.
In another case the C.N.R. graded the right of way from St. Walburg to Cold Lake and then did not lay the steel. There the right of way stands today, overgrown with trees. This lack of faith on the part of the Canadian National, this betrayal of many settlements in western Canada, is something that should be considered before we allow the Canadian National to say they are going to pull up this track. The railway should be made to live up to its responsibilities to the settlers, merchants and businessmen all along this line which the Canadian National is talking of abandoning.
These are some of the things to which the railway should give a close look, and to which we as legislators of this country should give a close look. I questioned Mr. Gordon in the railways committee with regard to this. He admitted that the salt mine was still there, but the settlers were still there, and he admitted the railway had betrayed them by allowing them to go in and settle these farmlands, then talk about abandonment. The possibilities are still there, but there is no talk of filling in the gap in order to make this a paying line so that it would be unnecessary to talk about abandonment.

I believe the Canadian Pacific was given running rights over the Canadian National from Prince Rupert to Debolt to complete the 90 miles to Debolt and tap the wealth of the Meadow Lake district. There it sits, with no hint of any extension because the railway has already tapped the wealth of the area, but they have deprived the people of Pierceland, Goodsoil and Cold Lake of access to a railway line. The Canadian National was forced to give the Canadian Pacific running rights on the 90 miles of track, and the Canadian Pacific only had to build 90 miles of track to tap the whole wealth of the Meadow Lake country.
These are some of the things at which I think this government should look before any such abandonment should be allowed. One knows very well that when the Canadian National had this line built to Debolt they were the ones who should have had the opportunity of tapping the Meadow Lake country. I am sure they could have made the line pay very easily. These are the things at which I feel we should have a close look before considering Bill No. C-120. We should consider the completion of these gaps that have resulted from mismanagement by the railways before the railways are allowed to go further in their betrayal of these people. When we stop to think that there is merely 38 miles of line to be completed between Frenchman Butte and Heinsburg to tap the wealth of that land and the salt mine in that area, then I believe the people in the area are entitled to have the line of which they have been deprived for many years. We should take another look at the line from St. Walburg to Pierceland, and the railways should get their heads together regarding running rights. Why should the Canadian Pacific have running rights over this track when they only need to build 90 miles of track to tap the wealth of the Meadow Lake country. They are leaving the people in the Goodsoil area with no chance of being any closer to a railway unless we make the railways sit down and talk some common sense before they talk about rail line abandonment.

Mr. Chairman, when the delegation presented its main case it consisted of opposition to any run-throughs at any time. There was quite a lengthy discussion and interview lasting two hours or two and a half hours on the first occasion. The second occasion was much shorter. Immediately following that, and arising out of the discussion-I am not sure of the date- they then brought forward a request for a postponement. This was a request for a postponement, not a counter-proposal to the one put forward by the railways. It did not involve any recognition or tentative admission that run-throughs would be agreed to at any time. This request, which was by itself, was immediately transmitted to the railway company. The railway management replied that they would consider it. There have been several discussions by the railway management. After discussion back and forth the railway has taken the stand that they do not think this partial implementation of the run-through on October 25, which is the main point discussed today, should be delayed. They do not believe it is appropriate to delay it.

Perhaps I could express it this way, although there is some danger in doing it, that out of a number of employees, say 90 employees, it would affect about 20 at the moment.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Is the minister satisfied that the railway management has observed the appropriate sections in the Montreal agreement of May, 1926?

I am not familiar with the Montreal agreement. The first time it was mentioned in any of these discussions was today. In addition there has been a great deal done that has not been required in law to be done. I am satisfied, notwithstanding some of the sharp criticism by hon. members today, about the generosity, if you like, of the offer to purchase homes from any of the men who wished to move, on the basis of a valuation of them and the implication of that in relation to the tax rolls of the community. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

Well, I will refer to some of these matters in a few minutes. The subject introduced today by the hon. member for Melville and the hon. member for Port Arthur is of major importance, and others who have spoken have drawn our attention to the fact that more instances like this are likely to occur in the near future. It is advisable for the committee to take cognizance of this situation. Perhaps some time during the course of this afternoon we may persuade the minister to communicate directly with the head of the C.N.R. and indicate to him the opinion expressed by members of parliament, suggesting a postponement of his proposed action would be very much in order so that further attention could be given to the problem and the wishes of the people of the community affected taken into consideration.
I do not see anything wrong in postponing an action such as this which, in its final effect, will be disruptive of the life of the community. We in this country are not opposed to modernizing our methods of transport. We have a progressive country and we want to proceed with many of these things. Everyone appreciates that the age of automation is crowding us closely, that disruption of the activities of many people is inevitable, but

Interim Supply
at the same time we think the blow should be eased as much as possible.
We have some experience in matters of this sort. A few years ago when I had some responsibility for uranium we negotiated an agreement with the United States on the basis of a stretch out program, so that the mining communities would receive another two, three or four years life before the shift occurred. The blow was eased a little bit, and there was not the sudden chop off in 1962 that was foreseen at the beginning of the negotiations.
The minister is familiar with the disruption of the T.C.A. overhaul maintenance base in Winnipeg. He knows the efforts he and his colleagues have made to stretch out the life of that base. I hoped that the base would not be transferred, but at the very least a stretch out program is essential when the lives of people are affected.
With such experience behind us why can the management of C.N.R. not adopt that principle? The minister has said the management must be given freedom to run its own affairs. Everyone is familiar with the answers we get to questions about crown corporations. A minister replies, "I will direct the attention of the crown corporation to the hon. member's observation or question." We get this all the time with the C.B.C., and over the years we have had the same experience with the C.N.R.
When crown corporations are dependant upon parliament for grants of money, and for modification of legislation that affects their operations, there must be a quid pro quo. We are justified in saying, "In return for the things we are doing for you, you must do something for us and our constituents, because we are dealing directly with the lives of people." The problem before us this afternoon affects the lives of people in a community that has been thriving for some considerable time.
On September 14, as recorded at page 7982 of Hansard for that date, the Minister of Transport expounded the philosophy that should prevail, and I quote:
It is our view that it is of great importance that we should give the railways an opportunity to operate as efficiently and as economically as possible and avoid adding unduly to fixed charges that are imposed upon the taxpayers and that inevitably have to be paid for and are therefore a minus factor in the economy. At the same time we must remember that the railways are large employers of labour; that the interests of the employees of the railways, our fellow citizens, must not be overlooked, and that, though change is essential in this field if the railways are to compete and receive a reasonable share of the traffic which will enable them to maintain their services out of 
their revenues, we must at the same time see that we do not, because of changes for which they have no responsibility whatsoever, visit hardships that are not reasonable and bearable upon a large section of the Canadian population.
That was a good expression of the philosophy that should be kept in mind when we are dealing with this type of problem. We should strive for economy and greater efficiency, but not at the expense of the people operating in the industry. Without people an industry just does not exist. It finally comes down to the human factor, and sometimes we tend to overlook the fact that the employee is a vital segment of industrial development. The employees of the railways are absolutely essential and their interests must be protected. As changes occur, those changes should be stretched out.
I question whether the management of the C.N.R. has lived up to an agreement which it signed on May 1, 1926. I am informed this agreement was signed by a representative of the C.N.R. and by representatives of the brotherhood of locomotive engineers and of the brotherhood of locomotive firemen and enginemen. It is known as the Montreal agreement, and I am told has been effective ever since. Section 9 of it reads as follows:
Nothing in this agreement shall be taken to permit the company without prior conference with representatives of the employees to change existing home terminal stations of the employees affected thereby

The action which it is proposed to take tomorrow interferes with that provision. It will change the existing home terminal station of the C.N.R. employees living in Nakina, and I ask the minister whether a prior conference took place between the C.N.R. management and the representatives of the two brotherhoods who were party to this agreement?
A few minutes ago the minister said he did not have the terms of the Montreal agreement in front of him.
Section 10 reads as follows:
This agreement will become effective when signed by the representatives of the Canadian National Railways, the brotherhood of engineers and the brotherhood of locomotive firemen and enginemen and shall continue in effect until 30 days notice of a desired change is given by either of the parties to the other.
I take it there are two requirements here -consultation and then formal notification from officials to officials, that is, from management to officials of the brotherhood, and it has not been clear this afternoon whether or not these two steps were taken. The suggestion has been left with us that unilateral

action was taken by the management of the C.N.R. If this is the case I suggest to the minister that an immediate phone call should be put through to the head of the C.N.R. with a recommendation that a postponement should take effect and that the status quo should remain tomorrow night. Then let the minister and railway management and the representatives of the brotherhoods get together and discuss whether or not this agreement of 1926 has been abrogated, and reach some *conclusion with regard to it. I think a definite responsibility rests on the minister in this regard. I am making no charges. I am asking for information. But it has been suggested to me that the steps to which I have referred, the steps contained in the agreement, have not been carried out. Parliament should know. If those steps have, indeed, been carried out, then the management of C.N.R. would not be under attack on that ground. If they have not been carried out, the management of the C.N.R. would, I think, have to give an accounting to parliament. We have some responsibility to the people of Canada for the way in which the railways are operated, and this is one matter I should like to see cleared up. Until it has been cleared up, I suggest the only reasonable approach is to postpone the action proposed tomorrow night.
I do not think the minister can put us off by saying: This is no concern of ours; it is up to management to carry on its affairs and we should not interfere. I say the management of C.N.R. should tell parliament what it is up to. I refer again to the statement by the Minister of Transport which I read a few minutes ago, the statement which says that hardships or burdens which are not reasonable should not be imposed upon a large section of the Canadian population.
Why this great haste with regard to the operation at Nakina? Why cannot suitable notice be given? Why cannot there be a stretch out program as suggested by the hon. member who spoke before me? Why cannot this operation be postponed until the spring of the year? How much difference would this make to the railway? Would it seriously inconvenience the railway? I doubt that very much. Will the people directly concerned be seriously inconvenienced, now that we are approaching the winter season? I think this is likely, and these are factors which I hope the minister will taken into account.
Other matters affecting the railways will be before parliament soon. Legislation concerning railway line abandonment to permit

greater economy and efficiency of operation will be a major subject for discussion. The railways will be expecting concessions and benefits as a result of the actions of parliament. In return we must say to them: Your employees and their families must be given a fair break. This is a good time to start, right now with regard to the problems which have come to our attention today. Let the management of the C.N.R. say right out: We will postpone our proposed change in Nakina, and subsequently give to the Minister of Transport, or to the acting minister, and through him to parliament, our proposals over a long period of time-so that parliament shall not be faced with isolated cases such as the one with which we are dealing today, but will have the general picture of what is proposed as a result of automation and the various changes considered necessary for efficient operation.

Why can we not have the whole plan put in front of us so that we may understand the general picture. And if railway management thinks we are presently unsympathetic, this is the way to cure that attitude. Give us the information, and then we shall be able to deal with these matters on the basis of accurate knowledge. We should not be faced with such a situation as occurred today-a motion for adjournment of the house on a matter of urgent public importance, raised because of a proposed action by railway management affecting the lives of people in Nakina whose protests had apparently been rejected. What recourse is open to them? Their only recourse is to appeal to members of parliament to raise the matter in the house, to bring it to the attention of the public and to urge the government to take some action.
This is, of course, what has happened today. We just happened to be dealing with interim supply when the subject could be discussed. May I say, in conclusion, that the minister himself is not unfamiliar with the activities of the government in connection with the railways, and employees of the railways, at various times over the years when strikes have occurred or when strikes have been threatened. The government has had to intervene. It has been obliged to consult and confer with representatives of both employers and labour. The minister has, I think, been through this process himself in the past. He will certainly remember the special session of 1950. I have vivid recollec-

tions of being up all night long, when we were in office, until 4 a.m. in the east block conferring with management and representatives of labour with regard to a proposed rail strike.
The government cannot avoid becoming involved in these problems which affect the citizens of this country. Why not take steps to head off trouble before it occurs? In this particular instance, action taken now might well forestall trouble later, though of course I do not know what other steps may be taken by those concerned. But in order to avoid a protracted dispute-and I gather this might happen from v/hat I have heard today-is this not an opportunity for the minister to take appropriate action immediately, to contact the head of the C.N.R., apprise him of the feeling of members of parliament, and to say to him: "Cannot we get a postponement of this?" Let us get all the facts assembled, if we have not already got them at our disposal, and see whether this matter cannot be cleared away without unnecessarily stirring up a hornet's nest. The minister can say to the head of the C.N.R.: "You are waiting impatiently for railway legislation to go through this house. If you proceed with this action you are not going to put the members of the House of Commons in the proper frame of mind to meet some of your requests in the future." I do not suggest that as a threat, but we are all human beings and we understand how these things operate. It is a quid pro quo. I make one final request to the minister to do his level best to get a postponement of the situation at Nakina.

Mr. Chairman, I shall just take a few moments of the time of the committee to speak on this subject of railways. First of all, I should say, in general reference to rail abandonment, that while in some circumstances conditions certainly exist where rail abandonment cannot be avoided and is in the national interest, it has always seemed to me that wholesale abandonment of rail lines indicates a lack of faith on the part of the railways in the future of this country. The fact that our growing population is now nearing 20 million means that in the future in all these areas more rail service will be required because these people will provide more rail traffic than has been the case in the past.
My primary purpose in rising this afternoon, however, is to discuss the question of the attitude of the Canadian Pacific Railway with reference to their policy of curtailing passenger service, specifically as it applies

to service by dayliners into and from the city of Halifax through the Dominion Atlantic run via the Annapolis valley to Yarmouth. As members of this committee will know, earlier this week the board of transport commissioners intervened to rule that the proposed curtailment of such service, which would have cut down the number of day-liners and the hours of service in that area for residents of the valley coming into and out of the city of Halifax, should be postponed until public hearings on the matter could be held. This occurred only after there had been widespread public protest. I am confident that when public hearings are held on this matter there will be very strong submissions, and well reasoned ones, against the curtailment of this service.
The only point upon which I wish to comment this afternoon is the fact that it appears to me, using this instance in Nova Scotia as an example, that the Canadian Pacific Railway is interested in getting out of passenger traffic rather than trying to make it pay, and that they are prepared to use whatever guise is necessary to make some of their runs unprofitable so that they can be abandoned. I can come to no other conclusion as a result of what is being done with this dayliner service in Nova Scotia.
Despite the fact that from Hants county and Kings county, which are areas served by the dayliner, as well as from other surrounding counties such as Lunenburg and Colchester, over 1,000 people drive their cars in all types of weather to commute to work in Halifax every day, people who would much sooner travel, particularly in the cold weather, in the comfort of an efficient commuter service, and despite the fact that these dayliners are very comfortable and satisfactory to the people who do have occasion to travel on them, the railway has never found it worth while to attempt to run dayliners during hours which would serve the commuting public in any manner, shape or form.
To give an example, the city of Kentville is about 69 miles from Halifax. All this summer and fall the dayliner service has been leaving Kentville in the mornings at something like 8.30 a.m. and arriving at Halifax at a quarter to eleven daylight time, which is the time in force in Nova Scotia at this time of year. I think you can readily see, Mr. Chairman, that this service cannot attract any but those who wish to travel in leisure at whatever hour they like and who are not working on that day. Now, if that train were

to leave Kentville at 6.45 in the morning and arrive in Halifax at a quarter to nine, although that might be a little late for people in the labouring class who start work at eight o'clock it nevertheless would be of great service to those who work in offices, banks, etc. who start work at nine o'clock in the morning. It does not take a great brain to see that the railway company could have much more in the way of traffic on that train if that were the case.
In addition, the train which leaves the city to go back to Kentville in the evening, the one they want to take off, has been leaving Halifax at a quarter to seven in the evening and arriving at Kentville a couple of hours later after passing through Windsor, Hants-port, Wolfville and other towns. I think it is obvious that if this service left downtown Halifax at, say, ten after five in the evening and made a stop on the outskirts of the city, particularly during the winter months, there would be a lot of people who would travel on the train.
However, I do not mean to suggest that at the present time this train travels empty or that the C.P.R.-D.A.R. application to curtail this service is justified. In the last couple of weeks and while this matter has been under consideration I have made a point of travelling on the train twice. I know that on a Saturday night coming from Halifax-I presume most people who leave the city for the week end leave on the Friday night-there were 38 people on board, which I am told is more than ample to justify its operation. On the week ends the service between Halifax and Kentville is very crowded. Acadia University students, and people at other educational institutions such as King's College, Edgehill and Haligonians going to the valley for one purpose or another, have patronized the service to the point that it has been extremely crowded at week ends. On another occasion during the past two weeks I travelled on the train when there were 140 people on board and I had to stand the whole way from Kentville to Halifax. I think this is a demonstration of the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway is interested only in getting out of the trouble of running passenger service.
Mind you, they are still talking of curtailment despite the fact that they are particularly busy on week ends and could make what I would call a continuous service at week ends when it pays handsomely. They arrange this service throughout the week and
Interim Supply
bring about a situation where, if a person goes out of or into the city he has no alternative but to stay overnight at his destination and return the next day. This type of commuter service could, I think, be a very efficient and profitable one if ran at the proper hours.
I think there is a responsibility somewhere to provide an efficient service. If the railways are not going to accept the proper responsibility, then it is the responsibility of some level of government-and I know of no other government than the one here- to work in co-operation with municipal officials in areas where rail service is run as part of a commuter service and is the only efficient commuter service serving the area concerned. The railways should consider the interest of the people in the cities. So much for the situation at Halifax.
I have brought this matter up this afternoon so that it receives some public attention before the hearings to which I have referred are held on this proposed rail curtailment, either later in the fall or early in the new year. I think the railways of this country are the foundation of our national existence.
The only other matter regarding the new rail legislation on which I should like to comment at this time is this. I hope I will be reassured by the officials of the government that when this legislation does reach the committee stage for consideration it will contain protection for the maritime interests, and the maritime interests I might add will not be protected as a result of leaving the Maritime Freight Rates Assistance Act as it is. That act, as some hon. members are aware, applies only to domestic cargoes. We are still faced with problems in respect of export and import cargo rates, if the ports of Saint John and Halifax are to remain in business, and that is something I am sure will be discussed in coming days.

Mr. Chairman, I should first like to congratulate the hon. member for Port Arthur and the hon. member for Melville for referring in the first instance to this matter. The fact that we have to discuss it during our consideration of interim supply is, of course, one of those things that happen in parliament. I am not going to refer to a decision that was made in this house today, particularly because I noted the chairman looking in my direction as soon as I referred to it, but I do not think there is any more important matter to be discussed by the members of the House of Commons at the present time than the subject we have been considering, and particularly its application to Nakina.
The railroad development that has taken place in this country is one of the most dramatic stories in Canadian history, as well as one of the most controversial. The minister today in his quiet way made some devastating revelations. After all, the matter that has been discussed is part of a larger problem in respect of automation, not only as it affects railways in this country, but as it affects other industry. The remarks placed on the record today indicate some lack of action and appreciation by those who sit opposite and who are charged with the responsibility of dealing with these matters. Railroad development in this country called together not only those men who formed the working unit of our railways, but the necessary resources to make our national railways system the utility it is today.
What has been suggested by the management of the C.N.R. in respect of Nakina is a modification of long term plans which were placed not only before the people of the various communities concerned, but the employees who were taken on as part of this organization. When we consider the extent to which the proposed action will affect many of these employees and communities, and the absolute lack of consideration for those who will ultimately be squeezed out, we cannot help but think that the House of Commons at this time could serve no better purpose than discussing this matter and impressing upon the government and the minister their responsibilities in this regard.
It has been said today that this matter is not directly part of the administrative responsibility of the ministry or government. That may be true in a narrow sense, but every one of us will agree that transportation

and railway problems, and problems associated with automation, must be of immediate concern to the ministry which sits in those seats across the way.
There are those individuals who will say that the railway officials have indicated to some that they will do certain things to help lessen the load, but there are others who ultimately will be squeezed out by this contemplated action. I have yet to note any contemplated action which will protect their interests in this matter.
When we consider interim supply we usually look for a grievance as the subject matter of our speeches. Today we did not have to look very far. Many things could have been referred to, but I think it is fitting today that we are discussing this subject which is related not only to personnel abandonment, which is one of the real problems facing the country today, but also to contemplated rail line abandonment. Without getting into a discussion of that aspect of the situation, as has been indicated by several members here today parliament itself should give an indication to the officials of the railways of the determination that the rights and privileges of their employees will not be forgotten. Nor will the future and welfare of the various communities concerned with rail line abandonments be forgotten.
We are told by the minister that there is complete flexibility, but it seems to me there is only flexibility so long as the C.N.R. is allowed to proceed on its chosen path, a path which the minister pointed out today is one which allows certain employees to bump others along the line. This is a procedure which will within less than two years affect the great percentage of the population of the town of Nakina.
The consequence of automation is one of the problems that everyone in the House of Commons and across this country is thinking about today. Every one of us realizes that with new techniques developed there will have to be a readjustment of our working force. We realize at the same time that in any readjustment, not only the companies involved but the government should move very carefully. What is taking place is an upheaval of our entire industrial process in Canada. With such an upheaval most families will necessarily find themselves in a new environment. The question we must ask at this time, and it has been asked by members of the opposition today, is whether or not those directly concerned and

affected by the action contemplated will indeed suffer a measure of inconvenience and loss out of proportion to what any citizen should be asked to shoulder.
The minister referred to the law. May I say to him that there is a law known as the law of common sense, and perhaps that is the kind of law that should govern in a case such as the one under consideration at the present time. A few months delay in this matter is of no great consequence to the C.N.R. but it is of great consequence to the men and their families, particularly having in mind, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the season of the year when the railway proposes to take this action. Indeed, sir, one would almost think that the management of the railway has forgotten entirely the inconvenience that will be suffered by their employees.
I do not want to take any more of the time of the committee this afternoon. I hope the minister will impress upon the officials of the C.N.R., particularly the president, the necessity for taking action to alleviate this situation, and I look forward to an announcement along that line, at least to the effect that the minister has tried. After the debate we have had today I suggest we have every right to expect that the minister should try to do something in this connection even at this late hour.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I want to express my complete support of the protests and pleas put before the house and the minister by the dozen or so members who have dealt with the proposals of Canadian National Railways, which will affect the lives of a good many of its employees and the welfare of certain communities. There is no necessity for me to repeat what they have so eloquently, forcefully and in some instances lividly stated.
I also want to express my complete support of the remarks made by the member on the government side of the house from Nova Scotia with respect to the Canadian Pacific Railway and its proposals for the abandonment of railway services and lines. I can see that the persons he represents are experiencing, shall I say, the same set of circumstances that the constituents I have the honour to represent experienced over a number of years. In my opinion the hon. member was quite correct when he said that in the first instance the C.P.R. does all it can to discourage passenger service and then uses the small numbers using the service as a
Interim Supply
reason for abandoning it. That is exactly what happened on the Kettle Valley railway.
For two or three years the C.P.R. did everything it could to decrease passenger service on the Kettle Valley railway by splitting the service at Penticton, by reducing the service and by making it as inconvenient as possible for the over 150,000 people served by that railway in the southeastern interior of British Columbia. While the C.P.R. has been successful in getting the board of transport commissioners to grant its application to withdraw passenger service on the Kettle Valley railway, in view of the fact that because of weather conditions and other circumstances numbers of people in the interior of British Columbia depend on railway travel primarily for good service in the winter, I suggest to the minister that this whole matter should be reconsidered and reviewed. I am not going to go into it at greater length now.
I want to take this opportunity to bring to the attention of the acting minister that this railway abandonment fever has again spread to the Kootenay district and is causing concern to the residents of the city of Rossland, and other people in my constituency. An application has been made by the C.P.R. to abandon some 7.1 miles of railway line between the village of Warfield and the city of Rossland. That is not a very long piece of railway line but it is an important one because it travels over a heavy grade into one of the highest cities in British Columbia, a city with a population of something over 3,000 people, a prosperous city which is mostly inhabited by persons employed by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, or persons who find their occupations in providing services to these employees. This application came out of the blue, as it were, and it has taken the people of Rossland by surprise.
I cannot understand the attitude of the C.P.R. first of all with respect to the Kettle Valley railway, which was and is a very profitable railway, although of course the C.P.R. insists on dividing freight receipts and passenger receipts, when presenting the company's costs. Second, I cannot understand the company's attitude now with respect to the abandonment of the line between Warfield and Rossland in view of the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway makes the bulk of its profits out of its operations in the Kootenays. I think the officials of that company completely fail to recognize their responsibility to the persons who are producing the greater part of

their profits, and I am sure there are a good many members of the house who will agree with me. I can see by the expressions on the faces of a number of members on the Progressive Conservative benches and on the government side of the house that I have a great deal of sympathy in respect of the plea I am making this afternoon.
Hear, hear.

I should also refer to the mutterings of approbation and so on expressed by Social Credit members to my rear. In this connection, Mr. Chairman, I now read a letter I received from the city clerk of Rossland. It is dated October 2, 1964, and reads as follows:
Dear Sir:
Re:	C.P.R. application for abandonment of
rail service Warfield to Rossland
Sorry for the delay in answering your letter of September 18 with regard to the above subject. After considerable study city council arrived at the decision that they would not object to the removal of the majority of track within the city limits-
See how reasonable they are.
-providing rail service is maintained from Warfield to the vicinity of the Rossland southerly boundary.
It is felt that in view of the renewed mining activity in this immediate area and in view of the fact that coal, flour and feed and a certain amount of oil and heavy equipment are supplied by rail the rail service should not be terminated to this city. There is 1.78 miles of main line and 1.21 miles of sidings within the city boundaries. Council would consent to this removal.
As a result of the correspondence I have received from the city of Rossland and other sources I have taken the matter up with the board of transport commissioners and I understand that an inspector has been sent to the district to interview the municipal authorities of Rossland, the major shippers in the district and all other persons who might be affected by this railway abandonment. I understand that after the inspector has reported to the board they will then come to a decision whether the circumstances are such as to warrant a hearing in the district with respect to the C.P.R. application to abandon this portion of their lines.
I urge the minister that in the first instance every opportunity be given to business people and other interested persons in the district to present their views at hearings of the board of transport commissioners, that a thorough study be made of the question and that there be no haste in coming to a decision. Here we have a very important industrial centre, the most important industrial centre in south-

eastern British Columbia, having to suffer once again from the railway abandonment fever which has seized the senior officials of the C.P.R. in recent years, and once again they have failed to recognize their responsibility not only to Canada as a whole but to the various employees and communities so seriously affected.

Mr. Chairman, we have had a very interesting discussion of this very vexing problem. When the hon. member for Port Arthur and the hon. member for Melville attempted to adjourn the house to discuss this very urgent matter their motion was not allowed, but still we have spent the whole day on this question which indicates just how important it is and how much it concerns most members of the house. This is the value of interim supply, that we can bring up these questions, as was pointed out by the Acting Minister of Transport when he argued against adjourning the house to discuss this matter. At that time he asked us to present our views and that is what we are attempting to do.
The acting minister gave quite a lengthy explanation of the railway company's attitude regarding the possible easing of the impact of the new policy upon the employees. It was quite a clear statement, but I do not believe it will allay all the fears of the railway workers. I should like therefore to join with others in congratulating the hon. member for Port Arthur and the hon. member for Melville for the introduction of this question, almost on the eve of what could be the adoption of this run-through policy. I do not want to repeat all the arguments because I believe most of the arguments concerning the impact of this policy on railway workers and communities have been advanced. However I feel I should take some part in this discussion, at least to the extent of pointing out that the main line of the Canadian National runs through my constituency of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. Since I will be referring to it a little later, I may point out also that the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway also runs through Moose Jaw-Lake Centre in the southern area. The Canadian National is in the northern area. It is for this reason I am joining in this debate to point out that many of my constituents are vitally concerned.
One of the main towns in my riding on the main line of the Canadian National is Watrous. There are a large number of railway employees there. I am sorry that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is away just now on official business, but I should like

to point out that a town in his constituency, Biggar, is also vitally concerned with this situation. I have received letters about it, Mr. Chairman, but I will not read them. They are from union officials, and although I have a few of them I should like to refer to some comments made in one letter. It deals with what is called the announced intention of Canadian National Railways to implement a change in operations which would require train crews to be on duty for double the length of time usually involved in making a run over twice the usual distance they have been required to operate. I quote:
We in the railway running trades, being most familiar with train operations, are very concerned over the unsafe condition that will result to both operating personnel and to the public if such a practice is permitted-
I just read that as an example of some of the letters I have received concerning this matter. The hon. member for Meadow Lake, as well as others, have made some reference to railway line abandonment. This is a matter of greater concern to western Canada perhaps, Mr. Chairman, because of the greater impact over a larger area. Now there is the added concern over this proposed policy of run-through. I agree with other speakers that technological advances cannot be stopped. We must advance, the railways must advance, the whole economy of Canada must advance and all industries must adopt technological changes.
However, I believe there are other considerations to offset considerations of railway efficiency or economy of operations. I am thinking of the effect of this run-through policy on individual workers as well as on the communities in which they now reside. The Acting Minister of Transport made a statement concerning the offer of the railway company to buy the homes of workers who are affected by the run-through policy and may have to move. This offer, I imagine, is appreciated to a certain extent, but it certainly is not the whole answer to the concern of railway workers. As others have said there is the disruption of home life, and as one earlier speaker said the attachment to the community is part of the home life. I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that the effect on the communities, should the railway workers have to move, is one of the main concerns in connection with this problem. I do not know the situation in Nakina too well, to which the hon. member for Port Arthur re-ierred. However, I do know the situation dn my home city of Moose Jaw, which is
Interim Supply
on the main line of the Canadian Pacific.
I think I should refer to it briefly, as I know what can happen.
The main line of the Canadian Pacific came through Moose Jaw in 1882. According to records there certainly was a great celebration when that first locomotive reached the small settlement of Moose Jaw. The city was established as the main divisional point on the main line of the Canadian Pacific between Winnipeg and Calgary. So many employees in the city were on the railway payroll that the city was referred to for many years as "Moose Jaw, the railway city". The main roundhouse was built there to service the steam locomotives, and a large proportion of the population was employed by the C.P.R.
The picture changed greatly with the advent of diesel locomotives. No longer was the roundhouse of use. The diesels could go right through without being serviced, and for the last three or four years the roundhouse was used for the storage of wheat. Many of the railway employees were moved to Winnipeg or Calgary, and the city is no longer known as the railway city.
Some years ago a large depot was built which is still in use. Right beside it was a big railway office filled with administrative staff, but now that building is nearly empty, except for the ground floor where the telegraph office is situated. I mention these things to indicate what the hon. member for Port Arthur is referring to when he forecasts conditions in Nakina.
However, during the last three years, due to the huge exports of wheat negotiated by the previous government, many railway employees were brought back to Moose Jaw. Also there is now the great potash development in Saskatchewan, and three or four of the big potash mines are located in my constituency. This development will create more business for the railway and bring more of its employees back to work in Moose Jaw. As a nostalgic gesture commemorating Moose Jaw as a railway centre, a public subscription was recently taken up to purchase a steam locomotive that used to operate out of Moose Jaw. It is now stationed in the city as a reminder of the older days before the big diesels and automation changed railway policy.
The employees are concerned about this policy of run-throughs because it is one more step in changing the mode of railway operations. We should consider the situation carefully, and I thought the hon. member for

Interim Supply
Winnipeg South Centre used a very apt term when he said this policy should be stretched out. The terms run pretty well together: Stretch out the run-throughs.
We should impress upon the government and the railways that no precipitate action should be taken. The run-through policy is supposed to go into operation on October 25, but I point out that Bill C-120, previously referred to, is designed to establish a rationalization authority, and I wish to emphasize the word rationalization. I might mention in passing that I could not attend a meeting today which dealt with Bill C-120, as I was waiting my turn to speak on these estimates. I have attended previous meetings in connection with that bill and the attendance at them indicates the great interest in the bill. In closing, Mr. Chairman, I believe the C.N.R. should be asked not to take this action until Bill C-120 is finally dealt with by parliament, at which time the house can take a look at the complete railway picture.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
On the occasion of interim supply members of the opposition have an opportunity to raise complaints about specific actions of the government, and in dealing with the subject matter being discussed today I wish to say it seems peculiar that the C.N.R., in a unilateral way, should be taking action against the town of Nakina. It is particularly peculiar when we consider some other aspects of government spending.
On this occasion interim supply involves something close to $800 million, and I would point out that the taxpayers of Canada support the C.N.R. to the tune of about $80 million a year. They also support the C.B.C. to the tune of about $100 million a year, and in view of these amounts it is most peculiar that the C.N.R. would take action practically to eliminate a town of some 400 wage earners and their dependants in an isolated part of northern Ontario, and this to save a few thousand dollars. It is even more peculiar because we know that in the not too distant future, if Bill C-120 is passed, it will implement an over-all pattern of operation for the C.N.R. We think this is quite justified, but having read the brief presented to the government by the delegation from Nakina I have come to the conclusion that it contained very strong arguments.
It is also worth noting that towns in the immediate vicinity also concerned with the functioning of the C.N.R. are in agreement with the terms of the brief. One of the towns which would probably benefit a great deal

as a result of this particular change is supporting the brief which was presented to the government. We must consider the social and human effects such a proposal is likely to have, even though the population directly involved might be considered small. It would be another matter entirely if we had the feeling that an over-all plan or policy was being introduced. But all we are getting are bits and pieces of policy. I must add that this is something for which the government itself has long been noted. Hon. gentlemen opposite try to tell us that this is a crown corporation, not subject to direct parliamentary authority, but we do not accept this view entirely because we know that in the interest of the people whose lives are affected the government could, if it wished, play a determining role.
I referred just now to failure to produce an over-all policy, and I would point in this regard to the present session of parliament, the longest I believe in Canadian history. We have witnessed one area of confusion after another. I see the Minister of National Health and Welfare in her place. We all know how many times she has tried to bring her pension plan before the house. Maybe she will be able to do so within a few days; I hope so. But one could examine any phase of government legislation during the present session and find confusion all the way. I referred earlier to the budget of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Here we find a creeping burden on the taxpayer. We find that increases in the expenditure of the C.B.C. have been very great, and undesirable to the people of Canada in many phases, though not in all phases, of the operations of the corporation. I must be fair in saying this criticism does not apply to all phases of the corporation's activities. The expenditure of money seems to mean nothing. I understand from my own research that the expenditures of the C.B.C. are now away beyond even those which are apparent; that the corporation uses methods to spend money in ways which have not been approved by parliament. We cannot get at this authority.
For the greater part of our discussion today the committee has been considering a proposal which would have an adverse effect on the people of Nakina and on the economy of that part of northern Ontario, and we must do something in this parliament to see that the rights of these people are fully protected and that they do not suffer as a result of the harsh policy which the C.N.R. is now adopting. The people who live in these railway towns are not the only ones who are uncer-

tain about their future. We need look no further than the Department of National Defence under this very government, and the uncertainty which prevails within that department at the present time. In addition to those in the Nakina area directly affected by the railway proposals, there are of course the small business people, the people who offer service in the stores and elsewhere, the police department, the school teachers, and so on. All these people are affected. It is all very well to offer a monetary return, but this does not really solve the problem. Does the C.N.R. intend to cut out these smaller towns right across the country, making all those concerned feel they do not know where the axe will fall next? I suggest that for once the government should take a decision. Let us take a small community of this kind and show the people of Canada that we intend to act in a democratic fashion. Let us not say: This affects only a few people so we do not need to worry about them; throw them out the back door. It is time we got down to serving the people of this country. If there is to be an over-all pattern, let us have it expressed in Bill C-120.
I was disappointed that only one hon. member opposite rose to support the views expressed by the opposition. I am referring to the hon. member for Halifax. I think sometimes that he should be over on this side of the house, but I will allow the hon. member to remain there as an outstanding member of the Liberal party, who can at least rise on occasion to criticize the policy being followed by his own government when he knows it is wrong.
In concluding these few remarks may I express the hope that the minister in charge of the Department of Transport will take another look at this situation affecting Nakina and take action to postpone or cancel the decision which the company has reached until at least such time as the house is able to consider Bill C-120.

I gather that most of the speeches made today have been directed to the minister who is piloting interim supply through the committee, the Acting Minister of Transport. I should like to direct a few remarks to him in his position as President of the Privy Council. May I say I am glad to see his colleague the Minister of Public Works present because the subject I am about to raise is of concern to his department, too.
I think the most expeditious manner in which I can place this question before the
Interim Supply
house-it is one which involves several departments and for that reason I raise it on interim supply-would be by reading the following letter which came into my hands today.
Dear Mr. Barnett:
I am sorry to have to call upon you once again. I hope this will be the last time.
My purpose in dealing with this letter is to try to ensure that it will be the last time, because I have had to do some troubleshooting before in this connection.
Last January we came to an agreement with the Department of Public Works regarding payment for land expropriated by the Department of Justice a year ago in August. To this date the agreement is all we have. Actual money does not seem to enter into their scheme of things.
To begin at the beginning:
1.	In February, 1963, we came to an agreement with the Vancouver office (of the Department of Public Works) regarding terms of sale of our land bordering the French Creek boat basin. Our offer was fully endorsed by the Vancouver office and forwarded to the Minister of Public Works in Ottawa. However, we received neither acknowledgement nor reply to our letter.
I might say that the project undertaken in connection with the sale is now proceeding. It is a good project, and I am happy to see it go on. Nevertheless, I think the other party concerned should not be left out in the cold. The letter continues:
2.	In August, 1963, without any previous warning, the Department of Justice expropriated our property and informed us after it had been re-registered. We had been assured by the Vancouver office that under no circumstances would this be done. You will understand our indignation, especially after we had been led to believe that our offer would be accepted.
3.	In January, 1964, our offer of February, 1963, was accepted and a cheque was received by Mr. Bruce Brown, Qualicum, solicitor for the Department of Justice. Naturally, we believed that interest was owing for the time lapse since expropriation and Mr. Brown withheld the cheque pending further word from the Department of Public Works.
4.	In February, they agreed to the payment of 5 per cent interest up until the time we received the money.
5.	In June, having heard nothing further I wrote to Mr. Walkey in Vancouver and his department assured me that our cheque had been mailed to Mr. Brown on May 26. By July, neither Mr. Brown nor I had received word of it. Again I wrote to Vancouver. This time they informed me that the Department of Justice had to get word from the department of the treasury before the cheque could come through. Mr. Brown wrote the Department of Justice immediately and they did not acknowledge even his letter. At the end of August he wrote again and this time the Department of Justice replied. They stated that they were waiting to hear from the Department of Public Works.
In September our lawyer in Vancouver was assured by the Department of Public Works that the delay had been caused by the E & N Railway rights

Interim Supply
but that everything was now cleared and that our cheque would be here within a few days. That was a month ago.
You will understand now why we have come to regard any statement made by any of the departments with distrust. My husband maintains that they should set up a department for activating other departments.
This matter is all tied up with my mother's estate. We are a family of five and we all think the situation has passed the ridiculous. Our lawyer agrees with us. What private individual or company would be allowed such inefficiency and actual dishonesty?
We would be grateful if you could take up the matter with the appropriate department-treasury, justice, public works? It is obvious that any individual's letter is beneath the notice of all of them.
Yours sincerely,
Mrs. M. Urie
I have put this letter on record in the hope that it may save the writing of another 20 or 25 letters on the subject, and also in the hope that the departments of justice, public works and the treasury will take due note of its contents. I also hope some immediate action will be taken to unsnarl this administrative tangle so that I will not have to follow through with the idea of proposing a motion to set up a department to activate other departments.

Mr. Chairman, as the hour is almost up now for the day, I should like to say a few words on this subject and possibly conclude my remarks on Monday. First of all I should like to say that I am shocked that it has been necessary to bring the situation which exists in Nakina up in this manner. We have had on the order paper since September 14 Bill No. C-120 which outlines the action planned by the government to provide for the country a national transportation policy. This bill has been on the order paper now for more than a month but still no action has been taken by the government to see that it comes before us for debate and the policies outlined considered so that we can determine whether or not it is good and helpful legislation and legislation which will be of benefit to the country.
Only recently in this house the Prime Minister, in answer to questions posed by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, assured us that the railway bill should be of assistance to the maritime provinces and that no detrimental action as a result of the bill would be forthcoming. However, I may say that the hon. member for Halifax indicated today that he was not anywhere near as optimistic about the legislation as was the Prime Minister. He is concerned about the Maritime

Freight Rates Act and the effect that this legislation will have on our area of the country. I may also say that Premier Stanfield recently indicated in a release that he was not anywhere near certain that the railway legislation was going to be of as much benefit as the Prime Minister would have us believe. Premier Stanfield indicated that a hike in freight rates for the Atlantic provinces would likely result from the new freight rate legislation now before parliament.
In view of the conflicting comments relating to this legislation, I am wondering whether or not it is the policy of the government to withhold any consideration of this matter until after November 9. I say this because a very important by-election is taking place in a very important railway centre in the maritime provinces. The city of Moncton derives a great deal of its livelihood from the operations of the C.N.R. and there is no doubt in my mind that there is a good possibility that what has happened at Nakina and what is possibly going to happen in Wain-wright might very well happen in Moncton.
This government does not want the constituents of Westmorland who will be putting their ballots in the box on November 9 to learn that this is going to happen in their area; to learn that there will be unemployment and people thrown out of work who now feel they have security and steady employment. No, this is not the type of thing this government wants those particular people to know about, so the government are leaving this legislation sitting on the order paper and taking no action on it in the hope that the people of Westmorland are not going to know anything about this, and that it will come as a great shock to them after they cast their ballots. This is done in the hope that if these people know nothing about it they will cast their ballots in favour of the Liberal party.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I think the Liberal party is going to get a shock because it is not going to get the benefit of the railway vote in the way hoped by pulling shoddy tricks like this, and not telling the people in the Moncton area that there is a very good chance, if this legislation is passed in the way it is presently framed, that they are going to be without jobs in a very short while. I think that the honest approach would have been for the government to bring this legislation before the house, to inform these voters what is actually going to happen in this area, and then let them decide what action to take at the polls on November 9.

This government will derive nothing but the deep distrust of the voters of Westmorland, and I certainly hope the voters react in the only way they can, and that is by showing this government on November 9 that this type of shoddy treatment is not what we in the maritime provinces expect, even though it is what we have been getting ever since this government has taken office.
May I call it five o'clock.
