The house resumed, from Friday, October 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Orlikow for the second reading of Bill No. C-43, to amend the Post Office Act (hate literature).

subsubtopic: USE OF MAILS FOR DISSEMINATION OF RACIAL DISCRIMINATION LITERATURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not in the house when my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) introduced Bill C-43 a week ago. However, I have read the debate and I wish to make a few remarks to urge the house to give second reading to this bill, or at least preserve the principles of it by adopting the suggestion made by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Klein), that this bill and others of a similar nature be referred for careful study to a committee of this house.
Mr. Speaker, I read very carefully the interesting speech of the Postmaster General (Mr. Nicholson) on this bill. He pointed out in his remarks the dilemma that faces anyone who is considering how to deal with a problem of this sort, and that censorship may be an evil greater than the disease it is supposed to correct. I myself as a lawyer, who has been interested over the years in civil liberties, think that we should not rush headlong into this suppression of freedom of
Post Office Act
speech or right to disseminate information merely because some material appears particularly odius or objectionable to us. I agree with the minister when he says that the courts are, generally speaking, the best places to determine what is legal or illegal and whether or not some particular publication goes beyond the boundary of tolerance. Although I share the hesitations of the minister, and I think these hesitations if I may say so are creditable, I think this particular bill deserves our support.
I believe it is necessary for us to have a balance in these matters, and I do not believe that the public or postal services of this country need be a vehicle for the hateful, dangerous and disruptive phenomena that we have seen in respect of this so-called hate literature. I think the evil is palpable as well as vicious. Even the most ardent champion of freedom of speech will recognize that a man who in a crowded theatre shouts "fire" has to be suppressed.
The minister himself told us he had found it possible to act under the Post Office Act in respect to scurrilous publications by proceeding under section 7. Can anyone doubt that in a shrinking world the most dangerous and most disruptive thing there can be in a human society is a matter which is calculated to bring into hatred, ridicule or contempt a person or group of persons by reason of their race, national origin, colour or religion-and I take those words from the bill introduced by my colleague. Nor do I think this language is too vague, or so broad as to invite interference with the rights of normal and healthy criticism. There is no real danger that just because on occasion one criticizes an individual or group of individuals there is likelihood of a postal ban being applied, if this legislation is adopted. I point out to the house that the ban applies only when the minister has reasonable grounds for believing that an attack contained in material is calculated to bring an individual or group into contempt by reason of race, national origin, colour or religion.
The minister told us that in the particular cases with which he had to deal he was able to conclude that the material in question offended some provision of the Criminal Code. I know, as do other members of this house, that the language of the Criminal Code is often necessarily very vague. In the field of sedition, for example, the classic definition uses language very similar to the language used in the bill before the house.

Post Office Act
The minister, quite rightly in my opinion, was hesitant about exercising the jurisdiction to decide what is offensive and what is scurrilous. I point out to the house that that duty is already imposed on the minister by the terms of the Post Office Act. All that Bill C-43 does is clarify what is offensive and what should not be allowed the use of the mails, by referring to that which creates hatred and contempt by reason of race, religion, and so on. There is nothing here to interfere with or stop in any way legitimate criticism of other groups. What is interfered with is something which must be calculated to bring individuals or groups into hatred or contempt.
There is nothing wrong with criticizing other groups of people, but it is when that criticism is based upon the fact of race or religion that it becomes disruptive of the society as a whole. Most of us in this house know what the effect has been of tolerance or indifference when this sort of poison is permitted. I see no reason why the public mails of this country should be allowed to be used for this type of very definite, very calculated and very real, if I may say so, menace we have seen at this time.
While I am speaking on this subject I should like to refer, without detail, to the sort of thing I mean. A distinguished member of the community from which I come, Rabbi Fein-berg is referred to in a pamphlet issued by a man named Stanley, as the "red rabbi". This pamphlet is published by the world service of Birmingham, Alabama, and distributed by Canadian publications. It refers, in tones that are definitely anti-Semitic, to a man who has rendered great service to his community. I must admit that he is a controversial figure, but the basic statements are without foundation. Why is it that on the back of this pamphlet the protocols of learned elders of Zion are advertised? This is something I think all hon. members of this house will know was used as almost a symbol of hate literature and violent racial poison. This advertising in itself attacks this distinguished rabbi of the community from which I come. We do not all happen to agree with Rabbi Feinberg, and he is a controversial man, but we know this sort of thing is scurrilous and insulting not only to him, not only to the particular race that he happens to represent, but to the whole community which he has served with distinction.
As I have said, I believe that while we should not jump headlong into more areas of censorship, and I would be the last to sug-

gest that should be done, I believe this particular bill defines, in clear enough terms, a clear and present danger, and that in all jurisdictions-in the supreme court of the
United States as well as others-the right of the community to deal with clear and present danger has been conceded as a proper exception to that general respect that we have and should have for freedom of speech.
The minister in this respect has no absolute discretion. His discretion is only in respect of making an interim order, and informing the people concerned, who have a right of appeal to a board of review. There are many other cases in respect of which we in this group have urged that ministerial discretions should be subject to a board of review. Under the Post Office Act they are. The minister was right in being hesitant about assuming this responsibility. I suggest he would discharge his responsibilities much better because he is hesitant. However, as he himself has said, he has had occasion already to deal with scurrilous literature. I do not see why this house should not strengthen his hands by passing this legislation.
I should like to conclude by saying that if the house feels that the actual wording of this legislation requires further study, if it feels there are implications about putting such provisions in the Post Office Act rather than in some other legislation which members wish to review, this can be done without our carrying on the spectacle of futility that sometimes happens when we merely talk out a bill of this sort. If the house is not ready to deal with this matter and give second reading to the bill I would hope we would accept the proposal made by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Klein) and preserve the basic idea on which I think we are all in agreement, that we must use what powers we have and can have to stop this hate literature. Therefore I hope this measure will be referred to a committee of the house, together with other bills that affect the same subject, so it will be clear that we are concerned and that we do realize the clear and pressing danger and propose to do something about it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
subsubtopic: USE OF MAILS FOR DISSEMINATION OF RACIAL DISCRIMINATION LITERATURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, everyone without exception detests this hate literature which is spread about the country by various means-through the mails or otherwise. I do not know anything more pernicious than this literature which reaches us through the mails, through newspapers, and which criticizes Jews, Protestants, Roman Catholics and other organiza-

tions because they do not entertain the same beliefs as the writers of such literature.
I think this is something we should abhor, something which should be removed from our statutes and our organizations, but this would be difficult because the mails are still secret. We have not yet come to the point of examining letters sent through the mails with a view to detecting hate literature, as is the practice in certain totalitarian countries. Furthermore, our postal employees, who are sometimes well-meaning, may not be quite qualified to examine seriously and thoroughly this literature which is addressed to us through the mails.
Many letters are sent from various post office boxes, various homes, various parts of the country, from the United States and elsewhere, and that literature is always as detrimental as the previous or the next one. It would be difficult for the post office and its employees to study and examine that literature and decide whether or not it should be intercepted. It would be difficult for the department to ask its employees to act in a totalitarian manner.
In my opinion, it would be preferable to examine this matter more thoroughly, and to obtain legal advice which would enable us to stamp out that literature. Those organizations are known to change their names and their postal boxes, and when reached in such and such a place, they are elsewhere and keep on sending us the same literature. If we were to amend every Canadian piece of legislation, we would not be any more able to prosecute the writers of such literature.
For the most part, this literature comes from the southern United States where Jews, Negroes and Asiatics are hated. I wonder whether it would not be advisable to refer this bill to a committee for careful and serious consideration, in order to see if there is some means of remedying this situation.

I know it has been very hard for the Postmaster General (Mr. Nicholson) and the postal officers to find the exact way to deal with this problem. It is an onerous one. It is one of the worst problems we have now or have had in the past, and I do not think we can find any easy way to deal with it. It is not that we do not hate this practice. We hate it just as much as anybody else does, but human nature being what it is there are only a few such crackpots throughout the country. They are crackpots in some ways, but 20220-595
Post Office Act
in other ways they know how to change their postal addresses and how to move from here to there. When we just about reach them here we find they are over there and we cannot reach them. So it is a difficult matter unless we can find some way to catch up and deal with all of them at one time. We cannot change the law every time they change their postal box number, so I think we need a committee to deal with the subject matter of such bills having to do with hate literature.
The government is most anxious that the whole subject of hate literature and all its ramifications be subject to the most searching scrutiny by a committee of the house. I believe that all parties in the house have at some time implied their agreement with such a proposal. When Bill No. C-21 dealing with genocide and group libel was before the house a government motion to refer the subject matter was turned down by certain opposition speakers. Since that time the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) himself has suggested in the house that the government should set up a committee to look into hate literature.
In view of all the public speeches purporting to be in favour of action in this regard, I now ask for unanimous consent to allow Bill No. C-21 to be dealt with at the same time as the bill now under discussion. To achieve this purpose I move, seconded by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai):
That Bills C-21 and C-43 be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on external affairs.
